topics.summary: Numbers organise our lives: we count, measure, pay and keep time with them. This chapter plays with numbers to see what else they can tell us.

content.text: Numbers are used in different ways to organise our lives: we count, measure, pay and keep time with them. In this chapter we play with numbers, see them around us, notice patterns and use them in new ways.
content.publication_text: Numbers are used in different ways to organise our lives: we count, measure, pay and keep time with them. In this chapter we play with numbers, see them around us, notice patterns and use them in new ways.

content.text: Math Talk: think of five different situations where you use numbers. Some ideas: reading the time, the date on a calendar, counting objects or marks in a test, measuring height and weight, paying money. Compare your list with a friend's. There are many more!

media.title: Two Line-ups and Their Taller-Neighbour Numbers
media.context: Shown as the concept opens, before the rule is given; students are asked what the numbers could mean and to compare a child who says 2 with the two children beside that child.
media.description: Under the heading "Two Line-ups and Their Taller-Neighbour Numbers", two horizontal panels display eight children of distinct heights standing on blue ground lines. In the top panel, labelled "First line", speech bubbles above the children read from left to right: "0", "2", "1", "1", "0", "2", "1", and "0". In the bottom panel, labelled "After rearranging", the same eight children stand in a different order with bubbles reading from left to right: "1", "0", "2", "0", "1", "2", "1", and "0". A logo and watermark read "SINGULARITY".
media.teaching_notes: Hold back the rule until several guesses are on the board. Point to each child who says 2 and ask what is true of both neighbours.

media.generation_prompt:
MATHEMATICAL IMAGE REQUIREMENT
Teaching purpose: Each child's number is the count of taller children standing right beside them.

Composition: Flat, friendly educational illustration for a middle-school maths lesson: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines (#2B2B2B), flat fills with no shading and no gradients, clean sans-serif labels in plain classroom English a child can read aloud. Colour-blind-safe colours: teal #0072B2 for the first set, amber #E69F00 for the second set, green #009E73 for what agrees or works, reddish purple #CC79A7 for the focus, grey #6B7280 for construction; muted red #D55E00 only for a wrong or impossible case, never as decoration. 16:9 landscape, 1456 by 816 pixels. Top panel: eight children standing side by side on one straight ground line, each with a speech bubble above the head holding one number. Bottom panel: the same eight children rearranged in a new order on a second ground line, each with a new speech bubble. Each child keeps the same clothes and hair in both panels so students can follow who moved. A short caption sits at the left of each panel.

Exact mathematical structure:
- Each panel shows exactly 8 children, all of different heights, feet on one straight ground line.
- Height ranks run from 1 (shortest) to 8 (tallest); every neighbouring pair shows a clearly visible height difference.
- Top panel, left to right, height ranks: 3, 1, 4, 5, 7, 2, 6, 8.
- Top panel bubbles, left to right: 0, 2, 1, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0.
- Bottom panel, left to right, height ranks: 5, 8, 2, 7, 4, 1, 3, 6.
- Bottom panel bubbles, left to right: 1, 0, 2, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0.
- The tallest child (rank 8) says 0 in both panels: right end of the top panel, 2nd from the left in the bottom panel.
- Each bubble points to exactly one child's head and holds a single numeral.

Visible text:
- 0
- 1
- 2
- First line
- After rearranging

Critical rejection conditions:
- a child with a 2 bubble is not shorter than both neighbours
- the tallest child in either panel does not have a 0 bubble
- the bubble numbers are not in the listed left-to-right order
- a child looks different between the two panels, so students cannot follow who moved
- two neighbouring children look the same height
- any count of objects, cells, ticks or dots that differs from the numbers stated above
- any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
- any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame

Student takeaway: Each child says how many of the children right beside them are taller.

media.description: Three panels show five children standing in line under the title "Three Possible Line-ups of Five Children". Each child has a numbered bubble above them. The left panel shows increasing heights with bubbles "1", "1", "1", "1", "0", labeled "Shortest to tallest" and "1, 1, 1, 1, 0". The middle panel shows heights "150 cm", "140 cm", "120 cm", "135 cm", "145 cm" with bubbles "0", "1", "2", "1", "0" and "0, 1, 2, 1, 0". The right panel shows heights "150 cm", "120 cm", "145 cm", "125 cm", "140 cm" with bubbles "0", "2", "0", "2", "0" and "0, 2, 0, 2, 0". A yellow star marks the tallest child saying "0" in each panel. Banners below read "The tallest child says 0" and "End children never say 2".
media.teaching_notes: Ask students to verify one bubble in each panel by pointing at the neighbours. Then ask why no panel could ever show 1, 1, 1, 1, 1.

maths_rules: a child says 2 only when both neighbours are taller, so an end child (one neighbour) never says 2; only places 2, 3 and 4 can say 2
of two children side by side with different heights, the taller one has a shorter neighbour, so the taller one cannot say 2; two neighbours never both say 2
places 2 and 3 are neighbours, and places 3 and 4 are neighbours, so place 3 cannot say 2 together with place 2 or place 4; the most is places 2 and 4, which is 2 children

the best line (the plan's heights) 150, 120, 145, 125, 140: 150 has one neighbour 120, not taller, says 0; 120 has neighbours 150 and 145, both taller, says 2; 145 has neighbours 120 and 125, neither taller, says 0; 125 has neighbours 145 and 140, both taller, says 2; 140 has one neighbour 125, not taller, says 0

media.title: Line-Up Lab
media.context: CBSE Class 6, NCERT Ganita Prakash Ch.3 'Number Play', section 3.1 'Numbers can Tell us Things'. Converted from the self-contained HTML build in output/maths/std6/Tools (tool_line_up_lab); the screen is the same 1600 x 900 stage drawn by the same code, with the children now real pictures.
media.description: Children of different heights stand on one ground line with their heights in centimetres at their feet. A bubble over each head shows how many of that child's neighbours are taller, and it updates live while a child is dragged along the line. Eight cards cover every question of NCERT 3.1, in order: find out what the numbers mean (six children in a park line saying 0, 2, 1, 1, 0, 1, answered by choosing the meaning); make the line say 1, 1, 1, 1, 0 (Q4); make it say 0, 1, 2, 1, 0 (Q6); get as many children as possible to say 2 (Q7, the most is 2); make both end children say 2 (Q1) and make every child say 1 (Q5), both impossible, answered with Impossible? and the right reason; can all the children say only 0s (Q2, answered 'Yes, if all the children are the same height', after which the five children stand at one height and all say 0); and make two neighbours say the same number (Q3). The finish card lists what each card showed, then free play lets the child change every input and watch the output at once: which three to six of six children stand in the line, each child's height (90 to 150 cm in steps of 5), their order (drag), and a fresh random line, with nothing to get right. One idea throughout: the number each child says is the count of taller neighbours, and it describes the POSITION, not the child.

tool_config.screen: One ground line with five children of different, clearly visible heights (heights in cm at their feet). A speech bubble above each head shows that child's number, updated live.
feedback: The tallest child always wears a soft glow, and that child's bubble is pinned at 0.
When a card is met, the matching bubbles turn green together.
A wrong 'Impossible' tap shows one arrangement that does meet the card.
tool_config.one_idea: The number each child says is the count of taller neighbours, and it describes the position, not the child.

student_controls.control: Drag a child to a new place in the line; the others slide to make room.
Read the live numbers after every move.
Work through the challenge cards one at a time.
On an impossible card, tap 'Impossible' and pick the reason: 'the tallest child always says 0' or 'an end child has only one neighbour'.

teaching_notes: Card 1 (NCERT p.55 'What do you think these numbers mean?'): six children in a park line say 0, 2, 1, 1, 0, 1 (the first five are the book's picture). The child drags them around (NCERT's 'the children now rearrange themselves') and chooses the meaning from three options; hint rung one is the book's own hint, 'Could their heights be playing a role?'. Only after this card does the tool state the rule.
Card 2 (Q4, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0): shortest to tallest; the tallest child always says 0.
Card 3 (Q6, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0): a short child in the middle, taller children at the ends.
Card 4 (Q7, most 2s): at most 2 of 5 children can say 2 (tall, short, tall, short, tall); the count of 2s under the ground updates live.
Card 5 (Q1, both ends say 2): impossible, reason 'An end child has only one neighbour.'
Card 6 (Q5, everyone says 1): impossible, reason 'The tallest child always says 0.'; the tallest child's bubble looks like every other bubble, so the child has to find the tallest by height.

Card 7 (Q2, all say only 0s): the child can try with five different heights first (it never works: the shortest child always has a taller neighbour), then answers. NCERT's answer is 'Yes, if all the children are the same height'; on the right answer the five children stand at 132 cm each and every bubble says 0.
Card 8 (Q3, neighbours match): two neighbours can say the same number, like the 1, 1 in the park line of card 1.
media.instructions_for_student: Drag a child to a new place in the line; the others slide to make room. Read the live numbers after every move. Work through the challenge cards one at a time. On an impossible card, tap 'Impossible' and pick the reason: 'the tallest child always says 0' or 'an end child has only one neighbour'.

content.text: Each child says the number of taller neighbours they have.

content.text: A child says 0 if neither neighbour is taller, 1 if exactly one neighbour is taller and 2 if both neighbours are taller.
content.publication_text: A child says 0 if neither neighbour is taller, 1 if exactly one neighbour is taller and 2 if both neighbours are taller.

content.text: Only the children standing right next to you count. A child in the middle has two neighbours, so can say 0, 1 or 2. A child at an end has only one neighbour, so can say only 0 or 1.
content.publication_text: Only the children standing right next to you count. A child in the middle has two neighbours, so can say 0, 1 or 2. A child at an end has only one neighbour, so can say only 0 or 1.

content.text: The number tells us about the child's place in the line, not about the child. A child who says 2 is shorter than both neighbours, so is a short child there, never a tall one.
content.publication_text: The number tells us about the child's place in the line, not about the child. A child who says 2 is shorter than both neighbours, so is a short child there, never a tall one.

content.text:
Example 1: Three children of heights 120 cm, 138 cm and 125 cm stand in that order. What does each say?
1. The first child has one neighbour, 138 cm, who is taller, so the first child says 1.
2. The middle child, 138 cm, has neighbours 120 cm and 125 cm, and neither is taller, so says 0.
3. The last child has one neighbour, 138 cm, who is taller, so says 1.
Answer: 1, 0, 1

topic_objective.objective_text: Students read the information a number carries, here how many taller neighbours a child has, and use the tallest child and the end positions to decide which number patterns are possible. A number tells us something only once we find the rule behind it.

to say 2 a child needs two neighbours, and both must be taller
a child at an end of the line has exactly one neighbour, so at most one taller neighbour, so says 0 or 1

concepts.concept_name: Numbers that Tell us Things: Q7

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M1.S3.T3.C18.IMG1}}
$1$. End children can never say $2$, so only positions $2$, $3$ and $4$ can.
$2$. Two children side by side cannot both say $2$, because one of them is the taller of the pair.
$3$. So positions $2$ and $4$ can both say $2$: tall, short, tall, short, tall.
Answer: At most $2$ children can say $2$, for example heights $150$, $120$, $145$, $125$, $140$.

Two children side by side cannot both say 2, because one of them is the taller of the pair.

video_script.anchor: Swap two digits of one number to get four supercells.
video_script.design: One idea: the four middle-edge cells share one neighbour, the centre, so shrinking the centre frees all four. Assumes: comparing five-digit numbers from the left, and the four-neighbour rule. Wrong idea: growing an edge number instead, which still gives one supercell. Transitions: the grid stays on the stage all video; the working band holds one line at a time; one hard clear of the working band before the recap.

video_script.wrong_move: A common slip swaps the 3 and the 9 in 39,344 to make 93,344. It becomes a supercell, but 62,871 now loses to it, so the grid still has only one supercell, 93,344. The slip's bubble is struck through.
maths_rules: The grid (book, end of chapter): top row 16,200, 39,344, 29,765; middle row 23,609, 62,871, 45,306; bottom row 19,381, 50,319, 38,408.
Neighbours are left, right, top and bottom only. The centre has 4 neighbours, each middle-edge cell has 3, each corner has 2.
Before the swap the only supercell is 62,871: it beats 39,344 (above), 50,319 (below), 23,609 (left) and 45,306 (right). Every middle-edge cell touches 62,871 and loses to it.
The slip: swap 3 and 9 in 39,344 to make 93,344. Checked by computer: then the only supercell is 93,344 (it beats 16,200, 29,765 and 62,871), and 62,871 loses to 93,344. Still 1 supercell, not 4.
The swap: exchange the 6 and the 1 in 62,871 to make 12,876. Checked by computer over every swap of two different digits in all nine numbers: this is the only swap that gives exactly 4 supercells.

The corners are not supercells: 16,200 loses to 39,344 and 23,609; 29,765 loses to 39,344 and 45,306; 19,381 loses to 23,609 and 50,319; 38,408 loses to 45,306 and 50,319. The centre 12,876 loses to all four.
Supercells after the swap: 39,344, 23,609, 45,306, 50,319, which is 4.

media.title: Supercell Builder
media.context: CBSE Class 6, NCERT Ganita Prakash Ch.3 'Number Play', section 3.2 'Supercells' (pp.57-59: the opening tables, Figure it Out Q1-Q10, Table 1 and the Try This Table 2) and the chapter-end Figure it Out Q1 (the 3 by 3 swap). Converted from the self-contained HTML build (_core/core.js + _src/tool_supercell_builder.js) and extended to the full section.
media.description: A supercell is a cell whose number is bigger than every number next to it, and a crown sits on every supercell. The intro shows the textbook's two opening rows (43 ... 34 and 200 ... 198) with their coloured cells. Eight levels, in order, covering every question, table and activity of NCERT 3.2. Level 1 (Q1): in the row 6828, 670, 9435, 3780, 3708, 7308, 8000, 5583, 52 the child taps every supercell and presses Check. Level 2 (Q2): the child fills 5346, _, _, 1258, _, _, _, 9635, _ with 4-digit numbers so the crowns sit exactly on the shaded cells 2, 4 and 9 (any valid filling is accepted). Level 3 (Q3, Q4): nine different numbers from 100 to 1000 for as many crowns as possible (5), then the child types how many supercells the table has. Level 4 (Q5): for rows of 2 to 7 cells the child types the most supercells possible; each answer draws a big-small row that proves it and fills a pattern table; then the child picks the method (start with a supercell, then take turns). Level 5 (Q6 to Q9): three reasoned choices on a sample row (can a table have no supercells, is the largest always one, can the smallest be one), then the cards 1 to 9: make 8 lose (Q8), then make 8 lose and 2 win (Q9, possible). Level 6 (more rows, Table 1): the child taps the four neighbours of 8632, then every supercell of Table 1. Level 7 (Try This, Table 2): the child builds each empty cell from the digits 1, 0, 6, 3, 9 so that only the coloured cells win, taps the biggest number, the smallest even number and the smallest number greater than 50,000, then puts the comma after the thousands digit. Level 8 (chapter-end Q1): one swap of two digits makes the four shaded cells of a 3 by 3 grid supercells. A miss never says wrong: it names why, outlines or flashes the cells involved, and the hint ladder climbs. Q10 (make variations) is free play: the child sets the layout (a row of 2 to 9 cells, or a grid of 2 to 4 rows by 2 to 4 columns), types any numbers 1 to 9999 into the cells or presses new numbers for a fresh random fill, and reads the crowns, the supercell count and the most possible for that size live.

teaching_notes: Intro: the book's opening rows. 79, 29, 34 and 626, 790, 198 are coloured: 626 beats 577 and 345; 198 has one neighbour, 109.
Level 1 (Q1): 6828, 9435 and 8000. An end cell has only one neighbour: 6828 wins at the left end, 52 cannot.

Level 2 (Q2): shaded cells 2, 4 and 9 must win and nothing else. The last cell must beat 9635 (e.g. 9636); both neighbours of 1258 must be below it. NCERT's filling: 5346, 5347, 1000, 1258, 1100, 1200, 1300, 9635, 9636.
Level 3 (Q3, Q4): at most 5 supercells in nine cells (cells 1, 3, 5, 7, 9), e.g. 110, 100, 150, 130, 280, 200, 230, 210, 270; Q4 answer 5.
Level 4 (Q5): the most for n cells is n/2 when n is even and (n+1)/2 when n is odd: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 cells give 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4. Method: start with a supercell, then small, big, small, big.

Level 5 (Q6-Q9): no table is without a supercell, because the largest number always wins (Q6, Q7); the smallest never wins (Q7); 8 loses beside 9 (Q8, e.g. 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 9 8); 8 loses and 2 wins with 2, 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 8 (Q9: possible).

Level 6 (Table 1): 8632's neighbours are 4580, 8280, 4795 and 1944. The book colours 7500, 9870, 8632 and 6034; 5785 (bottom left) also beats both its neighbours 4580 and 1944, so the rule gives five supercells and the tool says so.

Level 7 (Table 2): the top left cell must be 96,310. NCERT's filling gives biggest 96,310, smallest even 10,396, smallest above 50,000 60,193; the tool judges each against the child's own table. The child's numbers show bare until the comma step (96,310).
Level 8 (chapter-end Q1): swapping the 6 and 1 of 62,871 gives 12,876 and crowns the four shaded cells.

content.text: Two supercells can never sit side by side: of two neighbours, the smaller one is beaten.

maths_rules: A supercell is bigger than every cell it touches; an end cell touches one cell.
Comparing: more digits means bigger (670 and 52 are smaller than every 4-digit number); with the same number of digits, compare from the left.
Cell 1, 6828: only neighbour 670; 6828 > 670, supercell.
Cell 3, 9435: 9435 > 670 and 9435 > 3780 (9 > 3 in the thousands place), supercell.
Cell 5, 3708: 3708 < 3780 (3 = 3, 7 = 7, then 0 < 8 in the tens place), not.
Cell 9, 52: only neighbour 5583; 52 < 5583, not.
Supercells: 6828, 9435, 8000 (3 of the 9 cells).

maths_rules: The book's row has 9 cells: cell 1 = 5346, cell 4 = 1258, cell 8 = 9635; cells 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9 are empty (6 empty cells).
The coloured cells are cells 2, 4 and 9 (checked against the book page); every number must have 4 digits.
A coloured cell must be bigger than every neighbour; a plain cell must be smaller than at least one neighbour.
Cell 2 must beat 5346: choose 5347 (5347 > 5346).
Cell 3 is plain and must be smaller than 1258 so that 1258 can win: choose 1000 (1000 < 1258 and 1000 < 5347).
Cell 4, 1258, now beats cell 3 (1258 > 1000); cell 5 must be smaller than 1258: choose 1100.
Cells 5, 6, 7 are plain and climb: 1100 < 1200 < 1300, so 1100 loses to 1200 (and to 1258), 1200 loses to 1300, and 1300 loses to 9635.
Cell 8, 9635, is plain, so cell 9 must beat it: choose 9636 (any 4-digit number from 9636 to 9999 works); 9636 is an end cell and beats its only neighbour, so it is a supercell.
Full check of 5346, 5347, 1000, 1258, 1100, 1200, 1300, 9635, 9636: supercells are exactly 5347, 1258 and 9636, the 2nd, 4th and 9th cells.
the slip's cells 5 to 7: 1100, 1200, 1150; 1200 > 1100 and 1200 > 1150, so the 6th cell becomes a supercell, which is wrong.
The answer is one of many; any row where exactly cells 2, 4, 9 win is correct.

maths_rules: The book's table has 9 empty cells; numbers must be between 100 and 1000, with no number used twice (checked against the book page).
Two cells side by side can never both be supercells: the smaller of the two loses to the bigger one.
The slip row: 900, 800, 700, 600, 500, 400, 300, 200, 150; each cell after the first is smaller than its left neighbour, so only 900 is a supercell (1 supercell).
Take turns: big numbers in cells 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and small numbers in cells 2, 4, 6, 8.
The video's row: 900, 110, 800, 120, 700, 130, 600, 140, 500; every big number (500 to 900) is bigger than every small number (110 to 140), so each big cell beats its neighbours.
Why not 6: between two supercells there must be at least one plain cell; 5 supercells need at least 4 plain cells between them, 5 + 4 = 9 cells; 6 supercells would need at least 6 + 5 = 11 cells.
All numbers in the video's row are strictly between 100 and 1000 and none repeats.

maths_rules: The rule of the question: no number may be used twice.
For no supercells, every cell must lose to at least one neighbour.
The slip's row 12, 25, 31, 47, 58: each of 12, 25, 31, 47 loses to its right neighbour; 58 is an end cell and 58 > 47, so 58 is a supercell.

The biggest number in any row with no repeats is bigger than every other number, so it is bigger than each of its neighbours: it is a supercell whether it stands at an end (one neighbour) or in the middle (two neighbours).
Example with the biggest in the middle: 25, 58, 12 has 58 > 25 and 58 > 12, so 58 is a supercell.
Why the book forbids repeats: in 5, 5, 5 no cell is bigger than its neighbours, so that row has no supercells; repeats are the only way to avoid a winner.

maths_rules: The cards are 1 to 9, each used once; second largest = 8, second smallest = 2.
8 is not a supercell exactly when 9 sits next to it, because 9 is the only number bigger than 8.
2 is a supercell only if every neighbour of 2 is smaller than 2; the only number smaller than 2 is 1.
A middle cell has two neighbours and they cannot both be 1, so 2 must stand at an end with 1 as its only neighbour.
The video's row 2, 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 8: 2 > 1, its only neighbour, so 2 is a supercell; 8 < 9, its only neighbour, so 8 is not; the supercells are 2 and 9.

maths_rules: Ways to vary the puzzle: the number of cells, how many supercells, which cells are coloured, which numbers are allowed.
The slip's puzzle: 9 cells, 6 supercells; impossible, because between two supercells there is at least one plain cell, so 6 supercells need at least 6 + 5 = 11 cells; 9 cells hold at most 5.
The built puzzle: the cards 1 to 9, each once, exactly 4 supercells.

video_script.design: One idea: the four middle-edge cells share one neighbour, the centre, so shrinking the centre frees all four. video_script.wrong_move: A common slip swaps the 3 and the 9 in 39,344 to make 93,344. It becomes a supercell, but 62,871 now loses to it, so the grid still has only one supercell, 93,344. The slip's bubble is struck through.
maths_rules: The grid (book, end of chapter): top row 16,200, 39,344, 29,765; middle row 23,609, 62,871, 45,306; bottom row 19,381, 50,319, 38,408.
Neighbours are left, right, top and bottom only. The centre has 4 neighbours, each middle-edge cell has 3, each corner has 2.
Before the swap the only supercell is 62,871: it beats 39,344 (above), 50,319 (below), 23,609 (left) and 45,306 (right). Every middle-edge cell touches 62,871 and loses to it.
The slip: swap 3 and 9 in 39,344 to make 93,344. Checked by computer: then the only supercell is 93,344 (it beats 16,200, 29,765 and 62,871), and 62,871 loses to 93,344. Still 1 supercell, not 4.
The swap: exchange the 6 and the 1 in 62,871 to make 12,876. Checked by computer over every swap of two different digits in all nine numbers: this is the only swap that gives exactly 4 supercells.

The corners are not supercells: 16,200 loses to 39,344 and 23,609; 29,765 loses to 39,344 and 45,306; 19,381 loses to 23,609 and 50,319; 38,408 loses to 45,306 and 50,319. The centre 12,876 loses to all four.
Supercells after the swap: 39,344, 23,609, 45,306, 50,319, which is 4.

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M1.S5.T5.C26.IMG1}}
$1$. The $2\text{nd}$ cell must beat $5346$, so choose $5347$.
$2$. The $3\text{rd}$ cell must be smaller than $1258$ (and than $5347$), so choose $1000$.
$3$. $1258$ is now bigger than $1000$; its right neighbour must be smaller, so choose $1100$.
$4$. The $6\text{th}$ and $7\text{th}$ cells must not be supercells: $1200$ then $1300$ keeps each one beaten by the next.

content.text:
$1$. Two supercells can never sit side by side, because the smaller of two neighbours is beaten.
$2$. So the most we can get is by alternating: supercell, not, supercell, not, and so on, starting with a supercell.
$3$. $2$ cells: only the $1\text{st}$ cell, so $1$ supercell.
$4$. $3$ cells: the $1\text{st}$ and $3\text{rd}$, so $2$ supercells.
$5$. $4$ cells: the $1\text{st}$ and $3\text{rd}$ (the $4\text{th}$ is next to the $3\text{rd}$), so $2$ supercells.
$6$. $5$ cells: the $1\text{st}$, $3\text{rd}$ and $5\text{th}$, so $3$ supercells.
$7$. $6$ cells: the $1\text{st}$, $3\text{rd}$ and $5\text{th}$, so $3$ supercells.
$8$. $7$ cells: the $1\text{st}$, $3\text{rd}$, $5\text{th}$ and $7\text{th}$, so $4$ supercells.
$9$. Check for $7$ cells: in $50$, $10$, $60$, $20$, $70$, $30$, $80$ the supercells are $50$, $60$, $70$ and $80$, which is $4$.
Answer: $2$, $3$, $4$, $5$, $6$ and $7$ cells give at most $1$, $2$, $2$, $3$, $3$ and $4$ supercells: half the number of cells, rounded up.

$1$. The largest number is bigger than every other number, so it is bigger than each of its neighbours.

$5$. Example: in $40$, $15$, $62$, $30$ the largest, $62$, is a supercell (bigger than $15$ and $30$), and the smallest, $15$, is not ($40$ is bigger).
Answer: Yes, the largest is always a supercell; no, the smallest can never be one (in a row of two or more cells with no number used twice).

video_script.design: One idea: the thousands pick the gap, the rest says how far along it. Assumes: reading four-digit numbers and what halfway means. Wrong idea: two numbers with the same digits sit at one spot. Transitions: the line with its eleven marks and the two book numbers stays on the stage all video; the nine number chips wait above it and drop in one by one; one hard clear before the recap.
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip puts 5030 and 5300 at the same spot because they use the same digits; the picture shows 5030 only 30 past 5000 and 5300 a full 300 past it, and the single pointer is struck through.
maths_rules: The line runs from 1000 to 10,000 with equally spaced marks at 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, 5000, 6000, 7000, 8000, 9000, 10,000. Each gap is 1000.
Already placed (book): 2180 (180 past 2000, a little less than a fifth of the gap) and 2754 (754 past 2000, past halfway, since halfway is 2500).
Halfway between two marks is 500 past the smaller mark.
1050: between 1000 and 2000, 50 past 1000, very close to 1000.
1500: between 1000 and 2000, 500 past 1000, exactly halfway.
3050: between 3000 and 4000, 50 past 3000, very close to 3000.
3600: between 3000 and 4000, 600 past 3000, a little past halfway.
5030: between 5000 and 6000, 30 past 5000, very close to 5000.
5300: between 5000 and 6000, 300 past 5000; a third of 1000 is about 333, so 5300 is a little less than a third of the way.
8400: between 8000 and 9000, 400 past 8000, a little less than halfway.
9590: between 9000 and 10,000, 590 past 9000, a little past halfway; it is 10,000 - 9590 = 410 short of 10,000.
9950: between 9000 and 10,000, 950 past 9000; it is 10,000 - 9950 = 50 short of 10,000, very close to 10,000.

video_script.anchor: Five-digit numbers between 35,000 and 75,000 with only odd digits: which is the largest, the smallest, and the closest to 50,000?
video_script.design: One idea: build from the left, keeping inside the limits. Assumes: odd digits, comparing five-digit numbers, place value. Wrong idea: taking the biggest digits without checking the top limit. Transitions: the number line with its two limits stays on the stage all video, and each answer lands on it; five digit boxes sit in the working band; one hard clear of the working band before the recap.
never_show: a number starting with 4 as the closest
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip fills every place with the biggest odd digit after a 7 and says 79,999; on the number line it lands past the limit at 75,000, so it is outside the group. The number is struck through.
maths_rules: The group (book, end of chapter): five-digit numbers between 35,000 and 75,000 whose digits are all odd. Odd digits: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. No 0 can appear, so 35,000, 50,000 and 75,000 are not in the group.
Number line limits: 35,000 on the left, 75,000 on the right, 50,000 between them.
The slip: 79,999 > 75,000, so it is past the right limit.

Largest: first digit at most 7 (9 would give 90,000 or more). With 7 first, 75,111 is the smallest odd-digit number starting 75 and it is above 75,000, so the second digit must be less than 5; the biggest odd digit below 5 is 3. Then 9, 9, 9. Largest = 73,999, and 73,999 < 75,000.

Smallest: first digit at least 3 (1 would give less than 20,000). With 3 first, 33,999 < 35,000, so the second digit must be at least 5; the smallest is 5. Then 1, 1, 1. Smallest = 35,111, and 35,111 > 35,000.

Closest to 50,000: the first digit cannot be 4 (even) or 5 with a 0 after it (0 is even). Above 50,000 the smallest is 51,111: 51,111 - 50,000 = 1111. Below 50,000 the first digit must be 3, and the largest is 39,999: 50,000 - 39,999 = 10,001. 1111 < 10,001, so 51,111 is the closest.
Checked by computer over all 5-digit numbers from 35,001 to 74,999 with only odd digits: largest 73,999, smallest 35,111, closest to 50,000 is 51,111.

media.title: Tick Detective
media.context: CBSE Class 6, NCERT Ganita Prakash Ch.3 'Number Play', section 3.3 'Patterns of Numbers on the Number Line' (Figure it Out, p.59). Converted from the self-contained HTML build in output/maths/std6/cbse_eng_maths6_ch3_new (tool_tick_detective, M1.S7.T7.C47.2D1.html); the screen is the same 1600 x 900 stage drawn by the same code.
media.description: Four number lines from NCERT p.59, each with ten ticks of which only two or three carry labels. On each line the child first taps every gap between the labelled ticks (the 'Finding the step' card counts the gaps, then shows the difference, e.g. 2020 − 2010 = 10), then tries steps on the step dial (1, 2, 5, 10, 100, 1000). A trial step counts on from the first label in blue; a step that does not fit rings the label it misses and shows, above that tick, the value the step would have put there; the right step shows difference ÷ gaps = step. Then the child labels every remaining tick by typing its number (keypad or keyboard) into a blue box that moves from tick to tick; a number that belongs on another tick is named with its tick, anything else is told the neighbouring ticks differ by the step. Then the child circles the smallest number and boxes the largest. Line a has 2010 and 2020 two gaps apart (step 5), line b has 9996 and 9997 (step 1, running past 10,000), line c has 15,077, 15,078 and 15,083 (step 1, the middle label agrees) and line d has 86,705 and 87,705 (step 1000). Last, nine number chips are dragged onto a 1000 to 10,000 line where 2180 and 2754 are already placed: while a chip is dragged a zoom strip shows a small mark every 100, and after each drop a bracket shows how far off it was, naming the number whose spot it landed on when the same digits trick the eye (9590 and 9950, 5030 and 5300). The finish card lists what each line showed; free play then lets the child change every input of the idea (start label, step, how many ticks, the number to place) and reads the result out at once: every tick's label, the smallest (circled) and largest (boxed), the gaps, and where the number falls, nothing to get right.

tool_config.screen: One horizontal number line with ten ticks; two ticks carry labels, the rest are blank. A step dial and a chip tray sit below.
feedback: A wrong step makes the filled labels clash with a given label, which flashes red.
A chip snaps to its true position and a bracket shows how far off the drop was.
tool_config.one_idea: The step of a number line comes from two labelled ticks: difference ÷ gaps.
tool_config.done_when: All four lines are labelled correctly and at least eight chips are placed within one small gap of the true spot.

Turn the step dial (1, 2, 5, 10, 100, 1000) and watch the labels fill in.
Drag number chips onto the line to place them.

teaching_notes: Line a (2010 on tick 5, 2020 on tick 7): 2 gaps, difference 10, step 5; the line reads 1990 to 2035. The trap the dial shows: step 10 puts 2030 on the tick labelled 2020.
Line b (9996 on tick 4, 9997 on tick 5): neighbouring ticks, 1 gap, step 1; the line runs past 10,000, 9993 to 10,002.
Line c (15,077, 15,078 and 15,083 on ticks 1, 2 and 7): 6 gaps, difference 6, step 1, and 15,077 + 1 = 15,078 confirms it; 15,077 to 15,086.
Line d (86,705 on tick 4, 87,705 on tick 5): neighbouring ticks, only the thousands digit changes, step 1000; 83,705 to 92,705.

Placement (1000 to 10,000, a mark every 1000, 2180 and 2754 already placed): 1500, 3600, 9950, 9590, 1050, 3050, 5030, 5300 and 8400 go to their spots; a drop counts within 125 of its own spot and nearer to it than to any other number's spot. Same-digit pairs (9590 and 9950, 5030 and 5300) are the trap, and a drop on the other one's spot is named.

Label stage (NCERT 'label the remaining positions'): once the step fits, only the printed labels show; the child types the number for each empty tick (8 on a, 8 on b, 7 on c, 8 on d = 31 entries). Each entry is judged exactly against first label + (tick - first labelled tick) x step. A number that belongs on another tick is named ('2020 belongs on tick 7, not on tick 6'); any other number gets 'neighbouring ticks differ by the step'. The hint ladder never gives a tick's number.

video_script.anchor: Five-digit numbers between 35,000 and 75,000 with only odd digits: which is the largest, the smallest, and the closest to 50,000?
video_script.design: One idea: build from the left, keeping inside the limits. Assumes: odd digits, comparing five-digit numbers, place value. Wrong idea: taking the biggest digits without checking the top limit. Transitions: the number line with its two limits stays on the stage all video, and each answer lands on it; five digit boxes sit in the working band; one hard clear of the working band before the recap.
never_show: a number starting with 4 as the closest
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip fills every place with the biggest odd digit after a 7 and says 79,999; on the number line it lands past the limit at 75,000, so it is outside the group. The number is struck through.
maths_rules: The group (book, end of chapter): five-digit numbers between 35,000 and 75,000 whose digits are all odd. Odd digits: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. No 0 can appear, so 35,000, 50,000 and 75,000 are not in the group.
Number line limits: 35,000 on the left, 75,000 on the right, 50,000 between them.
The slip: 79,999 > 75,000, so it is past the right limit.

Largest: first digit at most 7 (9 would give 90,000 or more). With 7 first, 75,111 is the smallest odd-digit number starting 75 and it is above 75,000, so the second digit must be less than 5; the biggest odd digit below 5 is 3. Then 9, 9, 9. Largest = 73,999, and 73,999 < 75,000.

Smallest: first digit at least 3 (1 would give less than 20,000). With 3 first, 33,999 < 35,000, so the second digit must be at least 5; the smallest is 5. Then 1, 1, 1. Smallest = 35,111, and 35,111 > 35,000.

Closest to 50,000: the first digit cannot be 4 (even) or 5 with a 0 after it (0 is even). Above 50,000 the smallest is 51,111: 51,111 - 50,000 = 1111. Below 50,000 the first digit must be 3, and the largest is 39,999: 50,000 - 39,999 = 10,001. 1111 < 10,001, so 51,111 is the closest.
Checked by computer over all 5-digit numbers from 35,001 to 74,999 with only odd digits: largest 73,999, smallest 35,111, closest to 50,000 is 51,111.

final_answer.spoken: the largest is seventy-three thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine, the smallest is thirty-five thousand one hundred and eleven, and the closest to fifty thousand is fifty-one thousand one hundred and eleven

content.text: $5$-digit numbers between $35,000$ and $75,000$ have only odd digits. Find the largest, the smallest and the one closest to $50,000$.
content.question: 5-digit numbers between 35,000 and 75,000 have only odd digits. Find the largest, the smallest and the one closest to 50,000.
content.question_tex: $5$-digit numbers between $35,000$ and $75,000$ have only odd digits. Find the largest, the smallest and the one closest to $50,000$.
content.publication_text: $5$-digit numbers between $35,000$ and $75,000$ have only odd digits. Find the largest, the smallest and the one closest to $50,000$.

content.text:
$1$. Odd digits are $1$, $3$, $5$, $7$, $9$.
$2$. Largest: the first digit can be at most $7$; with $7$ first, the next digit must be less than $5$ to stay below $75,000$, so $3$; then $9$, $9$, $9$: $73,999$.
$3$. Smallest: start with $3$; the next digit must be at least $5$ to pass $35,000$, so $5$; then $1$, $1$, $1$: $35,111$.
$4$. Just above $50,000$ the smallest is $51,111$, which is $1111$ away.
$5$. Just below $50,000$ the largest is $39,999$, which is $10,001$ away.
Answer: Largest $73,999$; smallest $35,111$; closest to $50,000$ is $51,111$.

modules.brief_summary: A number can carry information about its place. Comparing numbers with their neighbours and placing them on a line are the first ways we read that information.
modules.detailed_summary: A number can carry information about its place. Comparing numbers with their neighbours and placing them on a line are the first ways we read that information.

modules.summary: Place value lets us count numbers without listing them, add up their digits, read them backwards and find the same patterns on clocks and calendars.

media.context: Shown after students predict the 2-digit count; they read down the rows to see why each count is ten times the one before.
media.description: A diagram titled "Choices in Each Place Give 9, 90, 900, 9000, 90,000" displays five horizontal rows labeled "1-digit", "2-digit", "3-digit", "4-digit", and "5-digit". An orange badge at the top reads "First place: never 0" with an arrow pointing down. Each row contains square boxes representing digit positions: one box in row 1 up to five boxes in row 5. The first box in every row is orange containing "9" with "1 to 9" underneath. Subsequent boxes are blue-bordered containing "10" with "0 to 9" underneath. To the right of each row are the corresponding products: "9", "9 × 10 = 90", "9 × 10 × 10 = 900", "9 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 9000", and "9 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 90,000".

<bookmark mark='q'/>What mistake do some students make here?
<bookmark mark='a'/>Some students say ten times ten, which is one hundred, for two-digit numbers.
They let the tens place be zero, so the number zero seven appears.
But zero seven is just seven, which has one digit.
A number never starts with zero, so the tens place has nine choices, not ten.
So nine times ten gives ninety two-digit numbers, because zero cannot come first.

media.context: CBSE Class 6, NCERT Ganita Prakash Ch.3 'Number Play', section 3.4 'Playing with Digits' (the table of how many 1- to 5-digit numbers there are, and Digit Detectives, book pages 60 to 61). The digit-sum questions of 3.4 ('Digit sums of numbers', Figure it Out Q1 to Q3) belong to the separate Digit-Sum Dials tool and are deliberately not in this one. Converted from the self-contained HTML build in output/maths/std6/cbse_eng_maths6_ch3_new (tool_digit_hunt_grid, M2.S10.T10.C62.2D1.html); the screen is the same 1600 x 900 stage drawn by the same code.
media.description: A hundred grid of the numbers 1 to 100 fills the left of the stage. Phase 1: the child taps a row of the grid to open it as a large zoomed strip, then taps every digit 7 on the digit itself (77 needs two taps, one for each place); three place counters (ones, tens, hundreds) and a sum add up to 10 + 10 + 0 = 20, and Done with a 7 still missing says only that some hide; the 2nd Done with 7s still missing makes them glow until they are tapped. Phase 2: for each place of the numbers 1 to 1000 the child types a prediction on the keypad, then a place wheel (a four-digit odometer) runs from 1 to 1000 and tallies that place hundred by hundred on a number line; a prediction that is not yet right runs the wheel through the first hundred only (up to 720 for the hundreds place) as the reason; a 2nd miss on the same place gives the answer 100 and the wheel counts it, and the three places add to 100 + 100 + 100 = 300. Phase 3: the child switches on the digits that can stand in the tens place (1 to 9) and in the ones place (0 to 9) of a 2-digit number, taps Check, then types 9 × 10 = 90 on the keypad. Phase 4 (NCERT's table): with the nine 1-digit numbers given, the child taps each empty cell of the table and types how many numbers have 2, 3, 4 and 5 digits on the keypad (90, 900, 9000, 90000); a solved cell shows its range (from 10 to 99 ...) and a × 10 chip links neighbours, and a value that is not yet right keeps the cell open with a reason. Phase 5: the child chooses digits to see where each is written on the grid and how often (a table of counts from 1 to 100) and answers that 0 is written least often (11 times); the surprise follows: 1 is written most often, 21 times, because of the 1 in 100. The finish card lists what each phase showed, then free play (reworked 2026-09-30): the child picks the digit (0 to 9) and sets the first and the last number counted (1 to 1000) with -100 -10 -1 / +1 +10 +100 buttons, or presses 'surprise me' for a fresh random digit and range, and everything follows at once: up to 100 the hundred grid shows every copy of the digit in its place colour (numbers outside the range fade), past 100 an odometer of the last number and a range bar take its place; the ones, tens, hundreds (and thousands) counters, the sum and a live sentence ('From 1 to 100, the digit 7 is written 20 times.') update on every change. Nothing is judged. One idea throughout: a digit is counted place by place, and each place adds its own share.

teaching_notes: Phase 1 (hunt the 7s, 1 to 100): 10 sevens in the ones place (7, 17, ..., 97) and 10 in the tens place (70 to 79): 10 + 10 = 20, none in the hundreds place. 77 is two taps, one per place. Done with 7s missing: the 1st time the pill says only that some 7s hide (no count, no place); from the 2nd time they glow and the child finishes by tapping them (her own success, not a reveal).

Phase 2 (the 1 to 1000 wheel): each place shows a 7 exactly 100 times and 1000 has no 7: 100 + 100 + 100 = 300. A prediction that is not yet right replays the first hundred (1 to 99, or 1 to 720 for the hundreds place) as the reason, then the child types again.
Phase 3 (2-digit numbers): the tens digit can be 1 to 9 (a 2-digit number cannot start with 0: 07 is just 7), the ones digit 0 to 9, so 9 × 10 = 90 two-digit numbers, from 10 to 99.

Phase 4 (NCERT's table, page 60): 1-digit numbers 9 (given in the book), 2-digit 90 (10 to 99), 3-digit 900 (100 to 999), 4-digit 9000 (1000 to 9999), 5-digit 90000 (10000 to 99999): largest minus smallest plus 1, and each extra digit gives 10 times as many. A cell that is not yet right asks for the smallest and largest k-digit number; the ladder then gives the example 100 and 999, the rule largest - smallest + 1, and the × 10 pattern.

Phase 5 (least and most, 1 to 100): 0 is written least often, 11 times (10 in the ones place, from 10 to 100, and the 0 in the tens place of 100); 1 is written most often, 21 times, because of the 1 in 100; every other digit is written 20 times.

topic_objective.objective_text: Students count how many numbers have 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5 digits, and how often a digit is written, by counting place by place instead of listing. Place value turns a long listing job into a short multiplication.

topics.detailed_summary: Place value lets us count without listing: how many numbers have 2, 3, 4 or 5 digits, and how many times a digit is written from 1 to 100 or 1 to 1000.
important_points: There are 9, 90, 900, 9000 and 90,000 numbers with 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 digits.
To count a digit, count each place separately and add; a number like 77 counts once for each 7.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students count the numbers with 1 to 5 digits as 9, 90, 900, 9000 and 90,000, using 9 choices for the first digit and 10 for every other place.
Students count how often the digit 7 is written from 1 to 100 and from 1 to 1000 by counting each place separately, so that 77 counts twice.
Students apply place-by-place counting to find every 7 in a hundred grid, sorting each by its place, and extend the count to 1 to 1000.

steps_tex: $1$-digit: $1$ to $9$ gives $9$.
$2$-digit: $9 \times 10 = 90$.
$3$-digit: $9 \times 10 \times 10 = 900$.
$4$-digit: $9 \times 10 \times 10 \times 10 = 9000$.
$5$-digit: $9 \times 10 \times 10 \times 10 \times 10 = 90,000$.

content.question_tex: How many times is the digit $7$ written from $1$ to $1000$?
content.publication_text: How many times is the digit $7$ written from $1$ to $1000$?

content.text:
$1$. Ones place: one $7$ in every ten numbers, $1000 \div 10 = 100$ times.
$2$. Tens place: $70$ to $79$ in every hundred, $10 \times 10 = 100$ times.
$3$. Hundreds place: $700$ to $799$, $100$ times.
$4$. Total: $100 + 100 + 100 = 300$.
Answer: $300$ times (and $20$ times from $1$ to $100$).

video_script.anchor: Digit sums of 40 to 70, and of 123, 234, up to 789: what pattern?
video_script.design: One idea: watch what each digit does. Assumes: adding single digits. Wrong idea: the digit sum always grows by one. The two questions stay in the anchor all video; the number table stays on stage for the first question and the row of three-digit numbers replaces it for the second; one clear, before the recap.
never_show: a 3-digit number after 789 with digits one after another going up
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip says forty-nine gives thirteen, so fifty must give fourteen; the digits of fifty are added on screen, five and zero make five, and the fourteen is struck in the warning colour
maths_rules: the digit sum is the total of a number's digits
Digit sums of 40 to 70, the 40s: 40 gives 4 + 0 = 4, 41 gives 5, 42 gives 6, and on up to 49, which gives 4 + 9 = 13; inside one ten the digit sum goes up by 1 each step
at 50 the ones digit falls from 9 to 0 (lose 9) and the tens digit grows from 4 to 5 (gain 1), so the digit sum drops by 9 - 1 = 8: 13 - 8 = 5, and 5 + 0 = 5
the 40s give 4 to 13; the 50s give 5 to 14; the 60s give 6 to 15; 70 gives 7 + 0 = 7; the drop is 8 at 50, at 60 (14 to 6) and at 70 (15 to 7)
the slip's 14 for 50 is wrong: 5 + 0 = 5
3-digit numbers with digits one after another going up: 123 gives 1 + 2 + 3 = 6; 234 gives 9; 345 gives 12; 456 gives 15; 567 gives 18; 678 gives 21; 789 gives 7 + 8 + 9 = 24
from one number to the next each of the three digits grows by 1, so the digit sum grows by 3
move 1 from the biggest digit to the smallest: 3, 4, 5 becomes 4, 4, 4, so 3 + 4 + 5 = 3 x 4 = 12; every such digit sum is 3 times the middle digit, so it is in the three times table
after 7, 8, 9 the next digit would be 10, which is not a digit, so the run stops at 789; the book's answer to will this pattern continue is no
digits one after another going down (321, 432, up to 987) give the same sums, 6 to 24
video_script.payoff_line: The digit sums are six, nine, twelve, fifteen, eighteen, twenty-one and twenty-four.

final_answer.spoken: six, nine, twelve, fifteen, eighteen, twenty-one and twenty-four, and the run stops at seven hundred and eighty-nine

media.context: CBSE Class 6, NCERT Ganita Prakash Ch.3 'Number Play', section 3.4 'Playing with Digits', sub-section 'Digit sums of numbers' (book page 60): Komal's example and Figure it Out Q1 (a to d), Q2 and Q3; answers checked against the chapter's answer section (Section 3.4, page 60). The table of 1- to 5-digit counts and Digit Detectives of the same section are in the Digit Hunt Grid tool (M2.S10.T10.C62.2D1). Converted from the self-contained HTML build in output/maths/std6/cbse_eng_maths6_ch3_new (tool_digit_sum_dials, M2.S12.T12.C69.2D1.html); the screen is drawn by the same code on the same 1600 x 900 layout.
media.description: Five vertical digit dials make a number: each dial has an up and a down arrow, can be dragged (drag down to bring the faint digit above the window in) or tapped on its faint upper or lower digit, and the four left dials have on/off switches; a 0 at the front is not written, so its dial switches off. A live meter shows the digit sum from 0 to 45 and the right panel shows the number, how many digits it has and its digit sum as a sum of digits. Goal 1 (NCERT Q1a): after Komal's 68, 176 and 545 (6 + 8 = 14, 1 + 7 + 6 = 14, 5 + 4 + 5 = 14, shown on the intro), the child makes and submits three different numbers of their own with digit sum 14; Komal's numbers and repeats are pointed out and not counted, any other number whose digits add up to 14 is accepted. Goal 2 (Q1b): the smallest number with digit sum 14 (59), starting from 194; a Submit with the right digit sum but not the smallest makes the dial to change glow, and the next time shows 59 beside the child's number. Goal 3 (Q1c): the largest 5-digit number with digit sum 14 (95,000), the same way. Goal 4 (Q1d): first a 5-digit number with digit sum 14 that has a 0 in it (a 0 adds nothing), then, on a keypad, three ever bigger numbers with digit sum 14 past 95,000 (each must be bigger than the last), drawn as a ladder of digit boxes with the zeros pale, then the question 'Is there a biggest number with digit sum 14?' answered No. Goal 5 (Q2): the number steps from 40 to 70 and the child types the digit sum of every number from 41 to 70 before the machine steps to it (40 is the worked start: 4 + 0 = 4); a sawtooth chart grows bar by bar and the meter shows each fall; then 'What happens to the digit sum each time a new ten starts?' (it drops by 8). The -8 marks, the drops count and the tens summary appear only once that is answered. Goal 6 (Q3): the digits of 123, 234, 345, 456, 567, 678 and 789 are consecutive; the child types the digit sum of each (6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24) into a table with a staircase chart (bars and totals; its +3 steps appear only once the pattern is answered), then answers 'Do you see a pattern?' (up by 3 each time, so all are multiples of 3) and 'Will this pattern continue?' (No: after 7, 8, 9 the next digit would be 10, which is not a digit). Every wrong answer shows why and allows a retry; hints climb a three-rung ladder. Then a finish card with stars and what was found, and free play: the same five dials, a target digit sum the child sets (a stepper, or tap or drag the flag on the meter), live read-outs of the number, its digit sum and whether it meets the target, and buttons that deal a new random number or a random number whose digit sum is the target. Nothing is judged there.

teaching_notes: Goal 1 (Q1a): many numbers share the digit sum 14. Komal's 68, 176, 545; the book's 248, 653, 356, 815, 833, 12335, 23351; any number whose digits add up to 14 counts (2707 of them fit on the five dials). The child makes three of their own; order and zeros do not change the digit sum.
Goal 2 (Q1b): 59. One digit cannot reach 14, so two digits are needed, and the smaller one goes in front: 14 - 9 = 5, then 9.
Goal 3 (Q1c): 95,000. The biggest digit goes in the highest place, then what is left (14 - 9 = 5), then zeros.

Goal 4 (Q1d): a 0 adds nothing to a digit sum, so zeros make a number bigger without changing its digit sum: 95, 950, 9500, 95,000, 9,50,000 and so on (the book lists 95, 9005, 900005, ...). There is no biggest number with digit sum 14: one more digit always gives a bigger one.

Goal 5 (Q2): the digit sums from 40 to 70 are 4 to 13, 5 to 14, 6 to 15, then 7. Inside a ten the digit sum rises by 1 (only the ones digit changes); at each new ten it drops by 8 (the ones digit falls from 9 to 0, minus 9, and the tens digit rises by 1): 49 gives 13 but 50 gives 5. This is the 'share your observations' part.

Goal 6 (Q3): 123, 234, ..., 789 give 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24. Each digit is 1 more than in the number before, so the sum grows by 3 each time; every sum is 3 times the middle digit, a multiple of 3. The pattern does not continue: after 7, 8, 9 the next would need the digit 10.

video_script.anchor: The smallest number with digit sum 14?

maths_rules: on the place-value chart each column is a place (ones on the right, then tens, then hundreds); the counters on a column are that place's digit
the digit sum is the total of the digits, so it is the total number of counters; here it is 14 counters
a column holds at most 9 counters, because no digit is bigger than 9
one column is not enough: 9 is less than 14
every 2-digit number is smaller than every 3-digit number, so the answer has 2 digits
to make a 2-digit number small, the tens digit must be as small as it can be, so the ones digit is as big as it can be: 9
14 - 9 = 5 counters go on the tens column; the number is 59; check 5 + 9 = 14
a tens digit of 4 would need a ones digit of 10, which is not a digit; tens digits 1, 2, 3, 4 would need ones digits 13, 12, 11, 10, none of which is a digit
the slip's 95 also has digit sum 9 + 5 = 14, but 95 is bigger than 59

final_answer.spoken: fifty-nine

video_script.substitution: Fourteen counters need two columns, and the tens column should get as few counters as it can.

video_script.anchor: Digit sums of 40 to 70, and of 123, 234, up to 789: what pattern?
video_script.design: One idea: watch what each digit does. Assumes: adding single digits. Wrong idea: the digit sum always grows by one. The two questions stay in the anchor all video; the number table stays on stage for the first question and the row of three-digit numbers replaces it for the second; one clear, before the recap.
never_show: a 3-digit number after 789 with digits one after another going up
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip says forty-nine gives thirteen, so fifty must give fourteen; the digits of fifty are added on screen, five and zero make five, and the fourteen is struck in the warning colour
maths_rules: the digit sum is the total of a number's digits
Digit sums of 40 to 70, the 40s: 40 gives 4 + 0 = 4, 41 gives 5, 42 gives 6, and on up to 49, which gives 4 + 9 = 13; inside one ten the digit sum goes up by 1 each step
at 50 the ones digit falls from 9 to 0 (lose 9) and the tens digit grows from 4 to 5 (gain 1), so the digit sum drops by 9 - 1 = 8: 13 - 8 = 5, and 5 + 0 = 5
the 40s give 4 to 13; the 50s give 5 to 14; the 60s give 6 to 15; 70 gives 7 + 0 = 7; the drop is 8 at 50, at 60 (14 to 6) and at 70 (15 to 7)
the slip's 14 for 50 is wrong: 5 + 0 = 5
3-digit numbers with digits one after another going up: 123 gives 1 + 2 + 3 = 6; 234 gives 9; 345 gives 12; 456 gives 15; 567 gives 18; 678 gives 21; 789 gives 7 + 8 + 9 = 24
from one number to the next each of the three digits grows by 1, so the digit sum grows by 3
move 1 from the biggest digit to the smallest: 3, 4, 5 becomes 4, 4, 4, so 3 + 4 + 5 = 3 x 4 = 12; every such digit sum is 3 times the middle digit, so it is in the three times table
after 7, 8, 9 the next digit would be 10, which is not a digit, so the run stops at 789; the book's answer to will this pattern continue is no
digits one after another going down (321, 432, up to 987) give the same sums, 6 to 24
video_script.payoff_line: The digit sums are six, nine, twelve, fifteen, eighteen, twenty-one and twenty-four.

final_answer.spoken: six, nine, twelve, fifteen, eighteen, twenty-one and twenty-four, and the run stops at seven hundred and eighty-nine

video_script.substitution: Watch each digit: which ones grow, and which one falls back to zero.

media.teaching_notes: Two questions share this video. The one idea: watch what each digit does. Inside a ten only the ones digit grows, but at a new ten it falls from nine to zero, so the sum drops by eight. With digits one after another, all three digits grow together, so the sum grows by three. A child who also lists three hundred and twenty-one up to nine hundred and eighty-seven gets the same sums and is right too.

content.question: Write other numbers whose digits add up to 14.
content.question_tex: Write other numbers whose digits add up to $14$.
content.publication_text: Write other numbers whose digits add up to $14$.

content.text:
$1$. Sample answer: any digits that add up to $14$, in any order, make a number with digit sum $14$.
$2$. Two digits: $7 + 7 = 14$, so $77$; and $8 + 6 = 14$, so $86$.
$3$. Three digits: $1 + 4 + 9 = 14$, so $149$; and $2 + 6 + 6 = 14$, so $266$.
$4$. Four digits: $3 + 2 + 5 + 4 = 14$, so $3254$.
$5$. Five digits, using a zero: $2 + 0 + 5 + 4 + 3 = 14$, so $20,543$.
$6$. Changing the order of the digits keeps the sum $14$, so $86$ gives $68$, and $149$ gives $194$, $419$, $491$, $914$ and $941$ too.
Answer: Sample answer: $77$, $86$, $149$, $266$, $3254$ and $20,543$ (there are many more).

content.text: What is the smallest number with digit sum $14$?
content.question: What is the smallest number with digit sum 14?
content.question_tex: What is the smallest number with digit sum $14$?
content.publication_text: What is the smallest number with digit sum $14$?

content.text:
$1$. One digit is not enough, because the largest digit is $9$.
$2$. Two digits must add to $14$; the tens digit should be as small as possible.
$3$. The ones digit can be at most $9$, so the tens digit is $14 - 9 = 5$.
Answer: $59$

content.text: What is the largest $5$-digit number with digit sum $14$?
content.question: What is the largest 5-digit number with digit sum 14?
content.question_tex: What is the largest $5$-digit number with digit sum $14$?
content.publication_text: What is the largest $5$-digit number with digit sum $14$?

content.text:
$1$. Make the ten-thousands digit as large as possible: $9$.
$2$. $14 - 9 = 5$ is left, so the thousands digit is $5$.
$3$. Nothing is left, so the rest are $0$.
Answer: $95,000$

content.text: How big a number can have digit sum $14$?
content.question: How big a number can have digit sum 14?
content.question_tex: How big a number can have digit sum $14$?
content.publication_text: How big a number can have digit sum $14$?

content.text:
$1$. $95$ has digit sum $14$.
$2$. $9005$, $900005$, $90000005$ still have digit sum $14$.
$3$. We can always add more zeros, so there is always a bigger one.
Answer: There is no biggest: we can always make an even bigger number.

content.text: Find the digit sums of $123$, $234$, $\ldots$, $789$.
content.question: Find the digit sums of 123, 234, ..., 789.
content.question_tex: Find the digit sums of $123$, $234$, $\ldots$, $789$.
content.publication_text: Find the digit sums of $123$, $234$, $\ldots$, $789$.

content.text:
$1$. $123$ gives $1 + 2 + 3 = 6$.
$2$. $234$ gives $9$, $345$ gives $12$, $456$ gives $15$.
$3$. $567$ gives $18$, $678$ gives $21$, $789$ gives $24$.
$4$. Each is $3$ more than the one before, because each digit went up by $1$.
Answer: $6$, $9$, $12$, $15$, $18$, $21$, $24$: multiples of $3$. The run stops at $789$, because $8$, $9$, $10$ is not three digits.

video_script.design: One idea: fix the ends, then vary the middle. Assumes: reading a number digit by digit. Wrong idea: using all three digits makes a palindrome; the backwards test breaks it. source: Book example: Write all 3-digit palindromes using the digits 1, 2, 3.
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip picks 123 because it uses all three digits; read from the right it is 321, not 123, so the number is struck through
maths_rules: A palindrome reads the same from left to right and from right to left; for 3 digits, the first digit equals the last digit and the middle digit is free.
Digits allowed: 1, 2 and 3, and a digit may be used more than once (the book's own samples 121, 313 and 222 repeat digits).
Book examples shown in the ground part: 121, 313, 222.
The slip's number 123 read from the right is 321; 321 is not 123, so 123 is not a palindrome.

video_script.anchor: Start with 34, add its reverse. Is the sum a palindrome?
video_script.design: One idea: reverse, add, check. Assumes: adding two 2-digit numbers in columns. Wrong idea: doubling the number instead of reversing it; the flipped tiles break it. Transitions: the start number and the rule card stay in the anchor all video; the column sum grows in the stage; one hard clear before the recap.
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip adds 34 to itself and gets 68; the digit tiles show that the reverse of 34 is 43, not 34, so the sum is struck through
maths_rules: The rule, from the book: start with a 2-digit number; add it to its reverse; stop if the sum is a palindrome, or else reverse the sum and add again. Each addition is one round.
The reverse of 34 is 43: the same two digits in the opposite order.
Column addition: units 4 + 3 = 7, tens 3 + 4 = 7, no carry; 34 + 43 = 77.
77 read from the right is 77, so 77 is a palindrome; the process stops after 1 round.
The slip: 34 + 34 = 68; the digits were not reversed. 68 is also not a palindrome (read from the right it is 86).
Your turn: start with 23; 23 + 32 = 55, a palindrome in 1 round; never shown or said.
video_script.payoff_line: Thirty-four reaches a palindrome in one round

final_answer.spoken: seventy-seven, in one round

video_script.substitution: Flip the digits to make the reverse, add in columns, then read the sum from both ends.

media.teaching_notes: One idea: the reverse is the same digits in the opposite order, and the rule is add, then check from both ends. Watch for children who double the number instead of reversing it, and for children who forget to check the sum before stopping.

video_script.anchor: Start with 76. Which palindrome do you reach, and in how many rounds?
video_script.design: One idea: reverse a longer number by reading every digit from the right. Assumes: reverse and add with a carry, and checking before stopping. Wrong idea: swapping only two tiles; reading the tiles from the right breaks it. Transitions: the start number and the rule card stay in the anchor; round one stays on the stage while round two is built beside it; one hard clear before the recap.
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip reverses 143 by swapping only the last two tiles and writes 134; reading every tile of 143 from the right gives 3, 4, 1, so the reverse is struck through
maths_rules: Round 1: the reverse of 76 is 67. Units 6 + 7 = 13, write 3, carry 1; tens 7 + 6 + 1 = 14. So 76 + 67 = 143.
143 read from the right is 341; 341 is not 143, so 143 is not a palindrome and we go on.
The slip: swapping only the last two tiles of 143 and writing 134; the true reverse is 341.
Round 2: 143 + 341. Units 3 + 1 = 4, tens 4 + 4 = 8, hundreds 1 + 3 = 4, no carry. So 143 + 341 = 484.
484 read from the right is 484, a palindrome; the steps stop after 2 rounds.
Your turn: start with 68; 68 + 86 = 154, 154 + 451 = 605, 605 + 506 = 1111, a palindrome after 3 rounds; never shown or said.

final_answer.spoken: four hundred and eighty-four, in two rounds

video_script.substitution: Read every digit from the right: the first and last digits swap, and the middle one stays put.

media.teaching_notes: One idea: the reverse of a 3-digit number reads all three digits from the right, so the first and last digits swap and the middle stays. Watch for children who swap only two neighbouring digits.

Round 2: the reverse of 132 is 231. Units 2 + 1 = 3, tens 3 + 3 = 6, hundreds 1 + 2 = 3, no carry. So 132 + 231 = 363.
363 read from the right is 363, a palindrome; the steps stop after 2 rounds.

maths_rules: Places, left to right: ten thousands (tth), thousands (th), hundreds (h), tens (t), units (u).
A 5-digit palindrome mirrors about the middle: tth = u and th = t; h is the middle and has no partner.
The number is odd, so u is odd: 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9.
t = 2 x u and h = 2 x t, so h = 4 x u. h is a single digit (at most 9), so 4 x u is at most 9, so u is 1 or 2.
u = 3 would give t = 6 and h = 12, which is not a digit.
u odd and u is 1 or 2, so u = 1; then t = 2, h = 4; mirror: th = t = 2, tth = u = 1. The number is 12421.
Check: 12421 read from the right is 12421; it ends in 1, so it is odd; t = 2 is double u = 1; h = 4 is double t = 2.
The slip's guess: u = 2, t = 4, h = 8, giving 24842; it ends in 2, so it is even and breaks the odd clue.

media.title: Reverse-and-Add Machine
media.context: CBSE Class 6, NCERT Ganita Prakash Ch.3 'Number Play', section 3.5 'Pretty Palindromic Patterns' (book pages 61 to 62: the opening numbers, All palindromes using 1, 2, 3, Reverse-and-add palindromes, Explore, Puzzle time; answers from the chapter's answer section, Section 3.5, page no. 61 and 62). Converted from the self-contained HTML build in output/maths/std6/cbse_eng_maths6_ch3_new (tool_reverse_add_machine, M2.S14.T14.C85.2D1.html); the machine phases are the same drawing code as the page, and the NCERT questions the page did not ask were added in the same style on 2026-09-29.
media.description: A reverse-and-add machine on one 1600 x 900 stage, with every question of NCERT 3.5 solvable on it. Phase 1 (palindromes): the book's five numbers 66, 848, 575, 797 and 1111 stand as cards; the child taps each card to drop its digits read from the right under it, with a mirror line through the middle, then answers 'What pattern do you see?' from three choices (each reads the same from both sides; not 'each is even', since 575, 797 and 1111 are odd; not 'each has 3 digits', since 66 has 2 and 1111 has 4). Part 2: the child types every 3-digit palindrome made with the digits 1, 2 and 3 on the keypad; 121, 313 and 222 are on a 3 x 3 board already, as in the book; each entry is checked (only 1, 2, 3; reads the same reversed, shown digit against digit; not already on the board) and drops into its place until all nine are found. Phase 2: the chapter's four additions, 34, 29, 48 and 76: Flip drops the reverse, and the child fills the column sum from the right one digit at a time, each digit checked as it is typed, with the carry written above the next column; the lamp lights and a mirror line splits the sum when a palindrome appears, otherwise Send back makes the sum the new number (Auto may finish a starter after its first round by hand). Phase 3: the child types 2-digit starters and runs them until one needs more than 3 rounds (69, 78, 79, 87, 88, 89, 96, 97, 98 or 99). Phase 4: the record, 89 or 98, runs 24 rounds to 8813200023188; then the Explore question: a board of all 90 two-digit starters that the machine runs, each cell coloured by the rounds it needed, and the child answers whether every 2-digit starter reaches a palindrome (yes). Phase 5: 196 runs to the machine's 30-round cap with no palindrome, and the child answers the book's question, are there numbers that never reach a palindrome (nobody knows for sure). Phase 6: Puzzle time: four clues and five place boxes (tth th h t u, as the book draws them); the child types a 5-digit number and each clue is checked on it (5-digit palindrome, odd, t double u, h double t) until 12421 fits all four, then picks the number in words (twelve thousand four hundred twenty one). Every step on the bar and every intro chip is a button that opens that step. The finish card lists what each phase showed; free play (reworked 2026-09-30) is a live lab with nothing to get right: the child types any starting number of 1 to 7 digits on the keypad (digit by digit, backspace, clear) or presses new number for a random one with 2 to 7 digits, and the tape of every reverse-and-add round, the round count and the palindrome reached (or the stop at the 30-round limit) redraw at once.

teaching_notes: Phase 1 (palindromes): 66, 848, 575, 797 and 1111 read the same from left to right and from right to left; such numbers are palindromes. The not-yet reasons are facts the child can see on the cards: 575, 797 and 1111 are odd, 66 has 2 digits and 1111 has 4. Part 2: a 3-digit palindrome has the same first and last digit, so with 1, 2 and 3 there are 3 choices for the ends and 3 for the middle: 3 × 3 = 9 (111, 121, 131, 212, 222, 232, 313, 323, 333). The board is laid out first digit by row and middle digit by column, so the gaps show what is still missing without naming it.

Phase 2 (the book's additions, page 61): 34 + 43 = 77 and 29 + 92 = 121 are palindromes in 1 round; 48 + 84 = 132 and 132 + 231 = 363, 76 + 67 = 143 and 143 + 341 = 484 take 2. Columns are added from the right; a column of 10 or more writes its ones digit and carries 1, and the last carry becomes a new first digit.

Phase 3 (try other numbers): only 10 two-digit starters need more than 3 rounds: 69, 78, 79, 87, 88, 89, 96, 97, 98 and 99. Small digits finish fast; starters whose digits add up to 15 or more are the slow ones.

Phase 4 (a large number of times; Explore): 89 and 98 take 24 rounds and end at 8813200023188, the 2-digit record. Then all 90 starters: 53 need 1 round, 22 need 2, 5 need 3, 4 need 4, 4 need 6 and 2 need 24, and every one reaches a palindrome, so the Explore answer is yes (the book's footnote: 'The answer is yes!').

Phase 5 (do some numbers never reach one?): 196 has no palindrome after 30 rounds (it has grown to 1400255515443103). Computers have gone much further without one, but nobody has proved it never comes: the honest answer is that nobody knows for sure ('For 3-digit numbers the answer is unknown. It is suspected that starting with 196 never yields a palindrome!').

Phase 6 (Puzzle time): the number is odd, so u is odd; t = 2u must be one digit and h = 2t must be one digit too, so u = 1, t = 2, h = 4; a 5-digit palindrome repeats them: 12421, twelve thousand four hundred twenty one. The tool checks the clues on whatever is typed and marks each one, so a child sees which clue a number breaks (12321: h is 3, not double 2).

topic_objective.objective_text: Students recognise and list palindromes, grow them by reversing and adding, and use the mirror structure to solve number puzzles. Palindromes show that the order of digits alone can give a number a pattern, and they lead to a question nobody has answered yet.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students define a palindrome, test numbers by checking that their digits mirror about the middle, and list all nine 3-digit palindromes made from 1, 2 and 3.
Students carry out reverse-and-add until a palindrome appears, count the rounds, and state that 2-digit starts always succeed while 196 is still unsettled.
Students use the mirror structure to solve the 12421 puzzle and to find the sum and difference of the smallest and largest 5-digit palindromes, then run reverse-and-add on new starts.

content.q_figure: Five boxes labelled tth, th, h, t and u from left to right, above a box headed 'Write the number in words:', with the clues: a 5-digit palindrome, an odd number, the t digit double the u digit and the h digit double the t digit.

content.text:
$1$. The number is odd, so the $u$ digit is odd: $1$, $3$, $5$, $7$ or $9$.
$2$. $h = 2 \times t = 4 \times u$, and $h$ is a single digit, so $u$ can only be $1$ or $2$.
$3$. $u$ is odd, so $u = 1$; then $t = 2$ and $h = 4$.
$4$. It is a palindrome, so the thousands digit equals $t$, which is $2$, and the ten-thousands digit equals $u$, which is $1$.
Answer: $12421$, twelve thousand four hundred twenty-one

video_script.anchor: Smallest and largest 5-digit palindromes: what is their sum, and what is their difference?
video_script.design: One idea: the first box cannot be zero, and the mirror pins the last box to it. Assumes: the mirror rule, and adding and taking away with carries. Wrong idea: all ones is the smallest; the zeros break it. Transitions: the question stays in the anchor all video; the five boxes stay through the ground and the first idea beat; the column sums replace them; one hard clear before the recap.
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip says the smallest 5-digit palindrome is 11111; the middle three boxes can hold zeros, so a smaller palindrome exists, and the number is struck through
maths_rules: A 5-digit number cannot start with 0; a 5-digit palindrome has first digit = last digit and second digit = fourth digit.
Smallest: the first digit must be at least 1, so first = last = 1; the three middle digits can be 0; smallest = 10001.
Largest: every digit 9; largest = 99999.
The slip's 11111 is a palindrome but bigger than 10001, because its middle digits are 1 instead of 0.

Sum, in columns: units 1 + 9 = 10, write 0 carry 1; tens 0 + 9 + 1 = 10, write 0 carry 1; hundreds and thousands the same; ten thousands 1 + 9 + 1 = 11. 10001 + 99999 = 110000 = 1,10,000 (one lakh ten thousand).
Difference, in columns: units 9 - 1 = 8; tens 9 - 0 = 9; hundreds 9 - 0 = 9; thousands 9 - 0 = 9; ten thousands 9 - 1 = 8. 99999 - 10001 = 89998 = 89,998.
video_script.payoff_line: Added, they make one lakh ten thousand, and taken away, they leave eighty-nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-eight

final_answer.spoken: one lakh ten thousand, and eighty-nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-eight

video_script.substitution: Only the first box cannot be zero, and the mirror makes the last box match it, so the smallest is 1 at both ends with zeros between.
video_script.wrong_answer: eleven thousand one hundred and eleven

media.teaching_notes: One idea: the smallest 5-digit palindrome keeps 1 at both ends and zeros in the middle; the largest is all nines. Watch for 11111 as the smallest (zeros are allowed in the middle), for 00000 (not a 5-digit number), and for lost carries in the sum.

content.text:

$2$. Largest $5$-digit palindrome: $99999$.
$3$. Sum: $10001 + 99999 = 1,10,000$.
$4$. Difference: $99999 - 10001 = 89,998$.

video_script.wrong_move: A common slip takes 1001 from 1111 as if they were ordinary numbers and gets 110; an hour has 60 minutes, not 100, so the answer is struck through
maths_rules: A palindromic time reads the same from both ends when the colon is ignored: 10:01 reads 1, 0, 0, 1.
In hour 10 the minutes would have to be 01, so 10:01 is the only palindromic time in hour 10. In hour 11 the minutes must be 11: 11:11. In hour 12 the minutes must be 21: 12:21.
10:01 to 11:01 is 1 hour = 60 minutes; 11:01 to 11:11 is 10 minutes; 60 + 10 = 70 minutes.
11:11 to 12:11 is 60 minutes; 12:11 to 12:21 is 10 minutes; 60 + 10 = 70 minutes.
From 10:01 to 12:21: 70 + 70 = 140 minutes, which is 2 hours 20 minutes.
The slip: 1111 - 1001 = 110, treating the clock like an ordinary number; wrong because an hour has 60 minutes, not 100.
Check: 140 minutes = 2 hours 20 minutes; 10:01 + 2 hours = 12:01; 12:01 + 20 minutes = 12:21.

Two thousand and thirty-two is a leap year too, with a twenty-ninth of February.
An ordinary year's calendar cannot fit a leap year, so the answer is two thousand and thirty-one.

maths_rules: 365 = 52 x 7 + 1: an ordinary year is 52 whole weeks and 1 day, so the next year starts 1 weekday later
366 = 52 x 7 + 2: a leap year is 52 whole weeks and 2 days, so the next year starts 2 weekdays later
1 January weekdays (checked): 2025 Wednesday, 2026 Thursday, 2027 Friday, 2028 Saturday (leap year), 2029 Monday, 2030 Tuesday, 2031 Wednesday
2031 is an ordinary year, like 2025, so every date falls on the same weekday: 2031 reuses the 2025 calendar, 6 years later
The slip's 2032 is wrong twice: 2028 pushes by 2, so 2032 starts on Thursday, not Wednesday; and 2032 is a leap year with 29 February
true general fact: an ordinary year's calendar comes back after 6 or 11 years, a leap year's after 28 years (for years 1901 to 2099); a gap of 5 years never works
