media.title: Palindrome Clock
media.context: CBSE Class 6, NCERT Ganita Prakash Ch.3 'Number Play', section 3.7 'Clock and Calendar Numbers' (book pages 64 and 65): the three kinds of clock times (4:44, 10:10, 12:21), Manish's and Meghana's birthday dates, the Try This on reusing a calendar, and Figure it Out Q2 and Q3. Figure it Out Q1 (Pratibha's 4, 7, 3, 2) and Q4 (5683's Kaprekar rounds) are covered by the chapter's Kaprekar Machine tool (M3.S19.T19.C100.2D1), by the coordinator's routing, and are deliberately not repeated here. Converted from the self-contained HTML build in output/maths/std6/cbse_eng_maths6_ch3_new (tool_palindrome_clock, M2.S17.T17.C95.2D1.html); the first, second, third and fifth steps are that page's four phases drawn by the same code, extended for full NCERT coverage.
media.description: A large digital 12-hour clock in seven-segment digits fills the left of the stage, with step buttons (−10, −1, +1, +10, +1 hour; keyboard arrows step one minute) and a green Stamp button; a strip keeps every stamp in time order with the minutes between, and marks in coral any wanted time the child steps past. Step 1 (NCERT Figure it Out Q3): from 10:01 the child stamps the next two palindromic times, 11:11 and 12:21, types on the keypad how many minutes each is from the stamp before (70, 70), then 'the one after that' from 10:01 (140). Step 2: every palindromic time from 1:00 to 2:00 (1:01 to 1:51), then how many palindromic times the whole 12-hour clock has (57: 6 in each one-digit hour, 9 × 6 = 54, plus 10:01, 11:11, 12:21), the clock staying free to explore. Step 3: every time like 4:44, all digits the same (1:11 to 5:55 and 11:11). Step 4: every time like 10:10, minutes that repeat the hour (1:01 to 9:09, 10:10, 11:11, 12:12, each 61 minutes after the last); a repeat shows a bar under the hour and a matching bar under the minutes. Step 5: three printed dates, predicted palindrome or not before a mirror shows the digits reversed (01/02/2001 is not). Step 6: the child types years and the mirror writes each year backwards as a day and month, to find every palindromic date from 2000 until today (8 as of 2026: all in February); then types full dates to find two dates like Manish's 20/12/2012, whose day and month make the year, from the past. Step 7: this year's calendar card beside a second year the child steps (1 January's day, 365 or 366 days, the whole of January), checked until the two calendars match (2026 matches 2037 and 2015). Step 8 (Q2): a table of the smallest and largest 5-digit palindromes, their sum and difference, typed cell by cell, a rejected entry keeping its reason beside the row. Every step can be opened from the step bar (the dots, bottom right), and Next always opens the next step not yet solved, so the finish card comes only when all eight are solved. The finish card lists what each step showed; free play (reworked 2026-09-30) has three views, each with its own inputs and a live read-out and nothing judged: the time (hour and minute steppers, a new random time, and the digits with their mirror, three pattern flags and the next palindromic time with its minutes away), a date (day, month and year steppers, a new random date, a jump to the next palindromic date, and the eight digits with their mirror), and two years (a stepper for each year, new random years, a jump to the next matching year, and the two calendar cards coloured where 1 January's day and the year's length agree).

teaching_notes: Step 1 (Figure it Out Q3): 10:01 reads 1001, a palindrome. The next palindromic times are 11:11 (70 minutes later) and 12:21 (70 minutes after that, 140 minutes after 10:01). With a two-digit hour the minutes are the hour written backwards.

Step 2: with a one-digit hour the time reads h, then two minute digits, so the last digit must be the hour and the middle one can be 0 to 5: 6 per hour (1:01 to 1:51). Hours 1 to 9 give 9 × 6 = 54, hours 10, 11, 12 give one each (10:01, 11:11, 12:21): 57 in all, the finish of NCERT's 'find all possible times' for the 12:21 kind. The book's answer also lists 05:50: written with a 0 in front, 0550 reads the same both ways, but this clock (like the book's own 4:44) writes 5:50, and 550 backwards is 055. The tool says so on screen when 1:10, 2:20, 3:30, 4:40 or 5:50 is stamped, when 8 (the count with a 0 in front) is typed, and after the count is solved.
Step 3 (the 4:44 kind): 1:11, 2:22, 3:33, 4:44, 5:55 and 11:11; 6:66 cannot exist because minutes stop at 59.

Step 4 (the 10:10 kind): the minutes say the hour again: 1:01, 2:02, ..., 9:09, 10:10, 11:11, 12:12, twelve times, each 1 hour 1 minute after the last. NCERT's answer section lists 10:10, 11:11, 12:12 and 09:09.

Step 5: a date is a palindrome when its eight digits read the same backwards: 11/02/2011 and 10/02/2001 are; 01/02/2001 is not (01022001 backwards is 10022010), although the printed solution lists it.

Step 6: a palindromic date is its year written backwards, so each year has at most one; from 2000 the month always comes out as 02, and the day (the last two digits backwards) must be 01 to 29: 10/02/2001, 20/02/2002, 01/02/2010, 11/02/2011, 21/02/2012, 02/02/2020, 12/02/2021, 22/02/2022 (the next is 03/02/2030). Manish's dates split the year into day and month: 20/04/2004, 20/06/2006, ..., 20/12/2012, and older ones like 11/11/1111. A year before 2000, a date that does not exist or one still to come prints its reason and is not a slip in the year hunt; in Manish's part it is.

Step 7 (Try This): two years share a calendar when 1 January falls on the same day and both have the same number of days. Each common year moves 1 January on by one day, a leap year by two. 2026 (Thursday, 365 days) matches 2015 and 2037; 2032 also starts on a Thursday but is a leap year.

Step 8 (Figure it Out Q2): smallest 5-digit palindrome 10001, largest 99999; sum 1,10,000; difference 89,998. A palindrome cannot start with 0, so the smallest starts and ends with 1. The sum and difference rows open once both palindromes are in; a rejected entry shows its reason (too many digits, not a palindrome, a smaller or larger one exists) beside its row.

content.text: Can we reuse a calendar?

content.text: Jeevan wonders why we change the calendar every year. Last year's calendar was different from this year's, and next year's will be different again.
content.publication_text: Jeevan wonders why we change the calendar every year. Last year's calendar was different from this year's, and next year's will be different again.

content.text: A year of 365 days is 52 weeks and 1 day, so the next year starts one weekday later. After a leap year of 366 days the next year starts two weekdays later.
content.publication_text: A year of 365 days is 52 weeks and 1 day, so the next year starts one weekday later. After a leap year of 366 days the next year starts two weekdays later.

content.text: A calendar can be reused when these shifts add up to a whole number of weeks (7, 14, ...) and both years are ordinary or both are leap years.

content.text: An ordinary year's calendar repeats after 6 or 11 years; a leap year's calendar repeats after 28 years.

content.text:
Example 2: Will the calendar for 2025 (an ordinary year) be reused, and when?
1. 2025 to 2026: shift 1 (total 1).
2. 2026 to 2027: shift 1 (total 2).
3. 2027 to 2028: shift 1 (total 3).
4. 2028 is a leap year, so 2028 to 2029: shift 2 (total 5).
5. 2029 to 2030: shift 1 (total 6).
6. 2030 to 2031: shift 1 (total 7), a whole week, and 2031 is ordinary.
Answer: Yes: 2031 uses exactly the same calendar as 2025.

video_script.anchor: The time is 10:01. How many minutes until the next palindromic time? And the one after that?
video_script.design: One idea: jump whole hours, then count minutes. Assumes: reading a clock and what a palindromic time is. Wrong idea: subtracting clock times like ordinary numbers; 60 minutes to the hour breaks it. Transitions: the clock and the question stay in the anchor all video; a time line from 10:01 is drawn in the ground part and grows through the idea part; one hard clear before the recap.
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip takes 1001 from 1111 as if they were ordinary numbers and gets 110; an hour has 60 minutes, not 100, so the answer is struck through
maths_rules: A palindromic time reads the same from both ends when the colon is ignored: 10:01 reads 1, 0, 0, 1.
In hour 10 the minutes would have to be 01, so 10:01 is the only palindromic time in hour 10. In hour 11 the minutes must be 11: 11:11. In hour 12 the minutes must be 21: 12:21.
10:01 to 11:01 is 1 hour = 60 minutes; 11:01 to 11:11 is 10 minutes; 60 + 10 = 70 minutes.
11:11 to 12:11 is 60 minutes; 12:11 to 12:21 is 10 minutes; 60 + 10 = 70 minutes.
From 10:01 to 12:21: 70 + 70 = 140 minutes, which is 2 hours 20 minutes.
The slip: 1111 - 1001 = 110, treating the clock like an ordinary number; wrong because an hour has 60 minutes, not 100.

media.title: Kaprekar Machine
media.context: CBSE Class 6, NCERT Ganita Prakash Ch.3 'Number Play', section 3.6 'The Magic Number of Kaprekar' (book pages 62 to 63: D. R. Kaprekar, the 6382 flow chart and table with its blank fourth column, 'Take different 4-digit numbers...', the Kaprekar constant 6174, and 'Carry out these same steps with a few 3-digit numbers. What number will start repeating?'), together with the chapter's Kaprekar exercises: 3.7 Figure it Out Q4 (how many rounds 5683 takes, page 65), 3.7 Figure it Out Q1 (Pratibha's largest and smallest 4-digit numbers, their difference and sum, pages 64 to 65) and 3.12 Figure it Out Q2 (how many rounds your year of birth takes, page 72). Converted from the self-contained HTML build in output/maths/std6/cbse_eng_maths6_ch3_new (tool_kaprekar_machine, M3.S19.T19.C100.2D1.html): the screen is the same 1600 x 900 stage drawn by the same code, then extended for full NCERT coverage.
media.description: A number machine on one 1600 x 900 stage. The start's digits sit in a tray of tiles; the child taps (or drags) them into row A, largest digit first, then into row B, smallest digit first, and presses Subtract: C = A − B is written with its leading zeros kept (0558 is a smallest number here, 5058 is questioned) and C's digits drop back into the tray for the next round. A full row that is not in order is questioned with the out-of-order tile ringed; tapping a tile in the row sends it back. After two rounds by hand, Auto may run the rest. Phase 1 reproduces the chapter's 6382 table (8632 − 2368 = 6264, 6642 − 2466 = 4176, 7641 − 1467 = 6174) and the child fills the chapter's blank fourth column by hand (7641 − 1467 = 6174 again: 'What happens if we continue?'); every finished run is then shown as the chapter's table, A, B and C = A − B per round. Phase 2 runs 5683 and asks how many rounds it took (typed on the keypad: 7). Phase 3: the child types their birth year, runs it and types its number of rounds, checked against the machine's own count. Phase 4 runs 2013, a start with a 0 (B = 0123). Phase 5 runs 3333 to 0000 and asks why it stops (A = B). Phase 6, 3-digit mode, runs 321 to 495 (198, 792, 693, 594, 495), then a 3-digit start of the child's own, and asks which number starts repeating (495). Phase 7 is Pratibha's question: her digits 4, 7, 3, 2 give 7432 − 2347 = 5085 and 7432 + 2347 = 9779; for each of four parts the child types 4 digits, builds the largest 4-digit number A and the smallest 4-digit number B (which cannot start with 0) and presses Subtract or Add, and the difference or sum is checked against the part's condition (greater or less than 5085 or 9779), so every valid choice of digits is accepted. The finish card lists what each phase showed; free play is a live machine (reworked 2026-09-30): each digit of the start has its own up and down arrows (or is typed on the keyboard), 4-digit or 3-digit mode, and new start makes a random one; every round (A, B and C = A − B), the number of rounds and the number the machine ends at are redrawn at once, with nothing to get right. Every step of the phase bar, and every step chip on the intro, opens that step.

A 3-digit C is shown with its leading 0 added.
Reaching 6174 (or 495) makes the trail glow and repeats the last round once to show it is stuck.

teaching_notes: Phase 1 (6382, the chapter's example): A = 8632, B = 2368, C = 6264; A = 6642, B = 2466, C = 4176; A = 7641, B = 1467, C = 6174. The chapter's fourth column is blank: the child runs it by hand, 7641 − 1467 = 6174 again, so the machine is stuck at 6174. Auto, if used for round 3, stops at 6174 so the fourth column stays the child's.

Phase 2 (5683, 3.7 Figure it Out Q4): 5085, 7992, 7173, 6354, 3087, 8352, 6174: 7 rounds. In round 2 the digits 8, 5, 5, 0 give B = 0558, because the machine keeps all four digits; 5058 is questioned. NCERT's answer section prints 8 rounds because it takes 5058 as B there (see notes).

Phase 3 (birth year, 3.12 Figure it Out Q2): any 4-digit year with at least two different digits; the child counts the numbered rows of the table (the 'again' row is not a round). 2014 takes 7 rounds, 1980 takes 3, 2006 takes 1; no 4-digit start takes more than 7.
Phase 4 (2013, a start with a 0): the 0 goes last in A and first in B: 3210 − 0123 = 3087, then 8352, then 6174: 3 rounds.

Phase 5 (3333): all four digits the same makes A = B, so C = 0000 and the machine stops; that is why the chapter asks for at least two different digits. The two other reasons (odd, too small) are answered with counterexamples (5683 is odd, 2013 is smaller, and both reach 6174).

Phase 6 (3-digit mode, the chapter's 3-digit question): 321 gives 198, 792, 693, 594, 495, and 954 − 459 = 495 again (NCERT's worked answer); then the child's own 3-digit start (100 gives 099, 891, 792, 693, 594, 495). The number that starts repeating is 495; every 3-digit start with at least two different digits reaches it within 6 rounds.

Phase 7 (Pratibha, 3.7 Figure it Out Q1): digits far apart make the difference large, digits close together make it small; large digits make the sum large, small digits make it small. B is the smallest 4-DIGIT number, so a 0 cannot stand in front here (0, 4, 7, 2 gives B = 2047), unlike the Kaprekar machine, which keeps 0247 as four digits. Each part is checked on its condition, not against one answer.

content.text: Two rules keep the magic working. First, the digits must not all be the same: 3333 gives 3333 - 3333 = 0.

video_script.design: One idea: see the design below. Wrong idea: using each middle number once and giving up at 26,500. Transitions: the anchor and the block column stay all video; the working band clears once, before the recap.

biggest middle number not above 28,000 is 25,000 (60,000 is too big)
The slip: 25,000 + 1500 = 26,500, then stopping, thinking 1500 cannot be used again; 26,500 is 1500 short of 28,000
another correct way, not shown: 13,000 + 13,000 + 400 x 5 = 26,000 + 2000 = 28,000
your turn: make 29,500; one answer is 25,000 + 1500 x 3 = 25,000 + 4500 = 29,500; never shown

media.context: Shown when subtraction is first allowed; students read the worked line and are asked how to make each of the four targets.
media.description: Under the heading "Six Number Boxes and Four Targets to Build", a light blue panel on the left displays six rounded boxes under a tag reading "Add or subtract". The boxes hold "40,000", "7000", "300", "1500", "12,000", and "800". On the right, five horizontal boxes present targets. The top box, with a green border, shows the worked example "39,800 = 40,000 - 800 + 300 + 300". The remaining four boxes, outlined in blue, display "45,000 = ?", "5900 = ?", "17,500 = ?", and "21,400 = ?".
media.teaching_notes: Point out that 40,000 minus 800 goes below 39,800 and the two 300s bring it back up. Let pairs try 45,000 before the walkthrough.

media.title: Target Builder
media.context: CBSE Class 6, NCERT Ganita Prakash Ch.3 'Number Play', section 3.8 'Mental Math', the building-numbers part (book pages 65 to 66: the figure with the middle column and the side numbers, its two worked examples, the Math Talk questions about 1000, 14,000, 15,000, 16,000 and which thousands cannot be made, and 'Adding and Subtracting'). The digits-and-operations part of 3.8 (its worked examples and Figure it Out Q1 and Q2) is the sibling Digit-Count Lab (M3.S24.T24.C140.2D1) and is deliberately not in this tool. Converted from the self-contained HTML build in output/maths/std6/cbse_eng_maths6_ch3_new (tool_target_builder, M3.S22.T22.C128.2D1.html); the screen is drawn by the same code on the same 1600 x 900 stage.
media.description: A 1600 x 900 stage: the Number Play header (title, phase title, hint, sound, home), a canvas card, and a footer with the caption bubble and the step bar. Phase 1 (the book's figure): the middle column 25,000, 400, 13,000, 1500, 60,000 stands between the eight side numbers (38,800, 28,000, 61,600, 31,000 on the left; 3400, 63,000, 19,500, 20,900 on the right) with the lines of the book's two examples drawn as arrows, and the child answers the book's question 'What can you say about the numbers and the lines drawn?' by choosing one of three statements; a statement that is not it gets a 'look again' line pointing at the lines, and the right one shows the worked examples 38,800 = 25,000 + 400 × 2 + 13,000 and 3400 = 1500 + 1500 + 400. Phase 2: the child makes each side number by tapping blocks (any block, again and again); a Target card, a Total card that says over or under by how much, a number bar with the target's flag and a Steps panel (repeats grouped, 1500 × 3) follow every tap, and any build that reaches the target exactly is accepted; undo, start over and 'Impossible?' (with a reason chooser) are always there. Phase 3: 14,000, 15,000 and 16,000 from the same blocks. Phase 4: 1000: the steps of 400 land on 400 and 800 and jump past 1000 to 1200 on the bar; the child taps Impossible? and picks the reason. Phase 5 ('What thousands cannot be made?'): the child makes 2000 and 3000, then taps every thousand from 1000 to 10,000 that cannot be made and taps Check; each mark is tested against what the blocks can really reach, a thousand marked that can be made turns green with its recipe (for example 7000 = 3000 + 2000 + 2000), and only 1000 is left. Phase 6 (Adding and Subtracting): new blocks 40,000, 7000, 300, 1500, 12,000, 800 with a + / − switch (or press and hold a block to take it away): the book's example 39,800 = 40,000 − 800 + 300 + 300, then 45,000, 5900, 17,500 and 21,400. Then the finish card (stars from the share of the 21 judged answers right first time, one finding per phase) and free play (reworked 2026-09-30: the child changes the target, the value of each of the five blocks, add only or add and take away, and how much one arrow tap changes; a 'new numbers' button makes a fresh set; the total, the gap to the target, the steps and whether the blocks can make the target at all update at once, and nothing is judged). Every segment of the step bar and every intro chip opens that step.

teaching_notes: Phase 1 (the book's figure, p.65): the lines show which middle numbers are added to make a side number, and a middle number can be used again and again: 38,800 = 25,000 + 400 × 2 + 13,000 (two lines from 400) and 3400 = 1500 + 1500 + 400 (two lines from 1500). The two statements that are not it: 'joined to its nearest middle number' (38,800 is joined to three different middle numbers) and 'a middle number can join only one side number' (400 is joined to both 38,800 and 3400).

Phase 4 (Math Talk, 'Can we make 1,000? Why not?'): 400 is the only block below 1000, and 1000 is not a multiple of 400: 400, 800, 1200 skip it. A reason that is not it says only why it does not fit ('a block can be used again and again' or 'the 400 block is smaller than 1000'); the second wrong reason says the answer ('steps of 400 skip 1000'), draws the three jumps on the bar and closes the step as shown, not solved.

Phase 5 (Math Talk, 'What thousands cannot be made?'): 2000 = 400 × 5 and 3000 = 1500 × 2, and every thousand from 2000 on is 2000s and 3000s put together (4000 = 2000 + 2000, 5000 = 3000 + 2000, ...), so only 1000 cannot be made; an exhaustive search confirms it up to 1,00,000. Check with nothing marked is a nudge, not a slip.

Phase 6 (Adding and Subtracting, p.66): with subtraction the child can go past a target and come back: 39,800 = 40,000 − 800 + 300 + 300 (the book's example), 45,000 = 40,000 + 12,000 − 7000, 5900 = 7000 − 800 − 300, 17,500 = 12,000 + 7000 − 1500, 21,400 = 12,000 + 7000 + 1500 + 300 × 3. Any signed build that reaches the target is accepted; the ladder points at the nearest block, then at taking a block away, then at the last three digits, then at the book's worked example 39,800 = 40,000 − 800 + 300 + 300 (a fourth rung).
media.instructions_for_student: Tap a block to add it (tap again to add it again). Long-press a block to subtract it (in +/- rounds). Undo the last step. Press 'Impossible?' and choose a reason when a target cannot be made.

topic_objective.objective_text: Students build target numbers mentally by adding, repeating and subtracting given numbers, and explain why a target such as 1000 cannot be made. Combining numbers flexibly is the heart of quick mental calculation with large numbers.

topics.detailed_summary: Make target numbers in our head by combining given numbers, using each as often as we like and, later, subtracting too. Some targets cannot be made, and we can say why.
important_points: Match the big part first, then fix the smaller part.
Numbers may be reused; with subtraction, overshooting and coming back is allowed.
A target is impossible when the small numbers cannot fill the gap exactly.

media.title: Digit-Count Lab
media.context: CBSE Class 6, NCERT Ganita Prakash Ch.3 'Number Play', section 3.8 'Mental Math', the part 'Digits and Operations' (book pages 66 to 67: the two worked examples, Figure it Out Q1 with its ten scenario cards and Q2 'Always, Sometimes, Never?'), plus the chapter-end Figure it Out Q6 (page 72: one 5-digit and two 3-digit numbers with sum 18,670). The building-numbers part of 3.8 (the arrow figure, 'Can we make 1,000? 14,000, 15,000, 16,000?' and 'Adding and Subtracting') is the sibling Target Builder (M3.S22.T22.C128.2D1). Converted from the self-contained HTML build in output/maths/std6/cbse_eng_maths6_ch3_new (tool_digit_count_lab, M3.S24.T24.C140.2D1.html); the screen is the same 1600 x 900 stage drawn by the same code.
media.description: A number lab for how many digits a sum or a difference can have. Two numbers, A and B, are each locked to a number of digits (2 to 5); each has an entry slot typed on the keypad or the keyboard, Min and Max buttons that jump to the smallest and the largest number with that many digits, and a slider. The result row shows the sum or the difference and a badge with how many digits it has; a table on the right lists the smallest and largest 2- to 5-digit numbers. Phase 1 rebuilds the book's two worked examples (12,350 + 24,545 = 36,895 and 48,952 − 24,547 = 24,405: the child types them in and freezes them; any pair that meets the condition is accepted). Phase 2 is NCERT's ten scenario cards: for each, the child either types or jumps to an example and freezes it, or taps Impossible; after a right Impossible the child taps which case proves it (the smallest or the largest), and after every verdict the smallest and largest cases are shown side by side. Phase 3 is the five always / sometimes / never statements; a wrong verdict loads a counterexample into the lab, and a right Never is followed by the same which-case-proves-it step. Phase 4 asks for one 5-digit and two 3-digit numbers that add up to 18,670 (three rows, Check). The finish card shows stars and what was found; free play (reworked 2026-09-30 after educator feedback) lets the child change every key parameter directly and see the result at once, with nothing judged: the digit count of A and of B (2 to 5), each number (keypad, Min, Max, slider, or -1 / +1), and + or −; a live sentence says how many digits that kind of card can have and how many the child's answer has, the result row and its digit badge update on every change, and the smallest and largest cases and the table of smallest and largest numbers (the rows of the two locked lengths tinted) stay on screen. New card makes a fresh random card and Reset goes back to 50,000 + 50,000. Update 2026-10-02: every judged question gives two tries, then the answer (the 1st wrong answer says only why; the 2nd shows one working way on a build question, or says the answer on a pick), and the last step ends with Finish and a celebration (confetti and a 'Well done!' card; no findings card, no free play button).

tool_config.screen: Two number sliders, each with a digit-length lock (2 to 5 digits) and Min / Max jump buttons, an operation toggle, a result with its digit count, and a verdict bar (Always / Sometimes / Never).
feedback: After a verdict, the tool shows the extreme cases that decide it side by side.

teaching_notes: Phase 1 (the book's examples, NCERT 3.8 'Digits and Operations'): 12,350 + 24,545 = 36,895 and 48,952 − 24,547 = 24,405, each a 5-digit answer from two 5-digit numbers. The lab opens on 50,000 + 50,000 = 1,00,000 (6 digits) and 50,000 − 50,000 = 0, so freezing too early shows why the digits of the answer are not fixed. After each freeze the extremes appear: 20,000 to 1,99,998 for the sum, 0 to 89,999 for the difference.

Phase 2 (NCERT Figure it Out Q1, ten scenario cards): seven cards have examples (the NCERT answer section's example is shown, small at the right end of the task card, after two wrong answers on the card; it is never loaded into the lab); three are impossible, and the child then picks the extreme that proves it: 4-digit + 4-digit never reaches 6 digits (largest 9999 + 9999 = 19,998), 5-digit + 5-digit never gives 18,500 (smallest 10,000 + 10,000 = 20,000), 5-digit − 5-digit never gives 91,500 (largest 99,999 − 10,000 = 89,999).

Phase 3 (NCERT Figure it Out Q2): a, b and d are only sometimes true (an example each way is shown); c and e are never true, proved by the largest case 9999 + 99 = 10,098 (only 5 digits) and the smallest case 10,000 − 99 = 9901 (already 4 digits). A wrong verdict says why it does not fit (an example where the statement holds or fails is loaded into the lab, or what 'sometimes' needs) and never the reason; after two wrong verdicts the answer is said.

Phase 4 (chapter-end Figure it Out Q6): 18,670 = one 5-digit + two 3-digit numbers. Two 3-digit numbers add up to 200 to 1998, so the 5-digit number is 16,672 to 18,470; 18,000 + 300 + 370 is one answer and any valid triple is accepted.
The idea throughout: the smallest and the largest cases fix every answer's range, so they decide in one step whether a card can happen at all.

never_show: a tick beside the slip's answer
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip splits 670 into 600 and 70; the box for 70 is a three-digit box with one empty place, so the answer is struck through in the warning colour
maths_rules: the target, as the book prints it (end of chapter): 18,670, made from one 5-digit number and two 3-digit numbers
3-digit numbers run from 100 to 999; two of them add to at least 100 + 100 = 200 and at most 999 + 999 = 1998
so the 5-digit number is from 18,670 - 1998 = 16,672 to 18,670 - 200 = 18,470; 18,000 lies in this range
The slip's split: 18,000 + 600 + 70 = 18,670, but 70 has 2 digits, so it breaks the rule
the chosen 5-digit number: 18,000; what is left: 18,670 - 18,000 = 670
670 = 300 + 370; 300 has 3 digits and 370 has 3 digits
another correct answer, shown in the recap: 18,170 + 250 + 250 = 18,670 (18,170 + 500 = 18,670)
the question has many correct answers; the book's answer key gives one

media.context: Shown as the concept opens, with the question: find the sum of the numbers in each figure; should we add them one by one, or can we use a quicker way?
media.description: Under a banner titled 'Three Number Patterns to Total: Rows, Dice and a Grid' with a 'SINGULARITY' logo, three panels labeled 'a', 'b', and 'c' present numerical patterns. Panel 'a' contains five interlocking rows: twelve orange cards showing '40' across three rows and ten blue cards showing '50' across two rows. Panel 'b' shows an 8 by 8 grid of 64 dice faces: 20 purple faces with five white pips forming five 2 by 2 blocks, and 44 teal faces with one white pip. Panel 'c' shows an arch-shaped grid with 32 blue cells showing '32' across four full rows, above 16 orange cells showing '64'.
media.teaching_notes: Let students count the cards, dice and cells before anyone multiplies. Ask which numbers repeat, how many times, and how they could check their count.

media.title: Group-and-Sum Board
media.context: CBSE Class 6, NCERT Ganita Prakash Ch.3 'Number Play', section 3.9 'Playing with Number Patterns' (book pages 67 to 68: 'Find out the sum of the numbers in each of the below figures. Should we add them one by one or can we use a quicker way?', figures a to f) and the end-of-chapter Figure it Out Q7 (page 72: 'Choose a number between 210 and 390. Create a number pattern similar to those shown in Section 3.9 that will sum up to this number.'). Converted from the self-contained HTML build in output/maths/std6/cbse_eng_maths6_ch3_new (tool_group_and_sum_board, M3.S27.T27.C171.2D1.html), which drew figures a, b, c and f; figures d and e were added so every figure of 3.9 is solvable. The screen is the same 1600 x 900 stage drawn by the same code.
media.description: All six figures of NCERT 3.9, drawn with the book's numbers, are summed by grouping, then the child creates a pattern of their own. In every figure the child selects tiles that show the same number, by drawing a stroke over them or tapping them, and presses Group; a group that mixes numbers is refused and the odd tile is ringed in red with the reason, grouped tiles fade so none is counted twice or missed, and the Groups panel lists each group as count × value (12 × 40 = 480). When every tile is grouped the keypad wakes, and the child adds the panel's lines and types the total (keypad or keyboard); a total that is not yet right is printed with a reason and the hint ladder, and the child types again. Phase 1: figure a, the staggered 40s and 50s (12 × 40 + 10 × 50 = 980). Phase 2: figure c, 32 × 32 + 16 × 64 = 1024 + 1024 = 2048. Phase 3: figure f, the rings round 1000 (4 × 500, 8 × 250, 18 × 125: 7250). Phase 4, the dice: figure b (an 8 × 8 board of dice showing 1 and 5: 20 × 5 + 44 × 1 = 144), then after 'next figure' figure d (7 × 5 dice showing 3 and 4: 17 × 3 + 18 × 4 = 123); each die counts as its dots. Phase 5: figure e, the big hexagon of seven hexagons and six rhombi with a 15, 25 or 35 in each corner (22 of each: 330 + 550 + 770 = 1650); each number answers anywhere in its corner, so one stroke round a hexagon picks its six numbers. Phase 6 (end-of-chapter Figure it Out Q7): the child sets a target from 210 to 390 with -10/+10 and builds a pattern on a mirrored 4 × 5 board, where a tile placed on one side appears on the other and the middle line holds single tiles; any board whose sum equals the target is accepted (NCERT's own 250 = 25, 25 / 50, 50, 50 / 25, 25 works). The finish card lists what each phase showed, then free play lets the child change every key parameter and see the result at once, with nothing to get right: how many tiles of each of up to four numbers, each number (1 to 99), the board's rows (1 to 5) and columns (1 to 8), or a new random board; the groups (count × value), each product and the total update on every change. One idea throughout: a patterned sum is groups times value, so structure replaces adding one by one.

teaching_notes: Phase 1 (figure a): 12 tiles of 40 and 10 of 50 in staggered rows; 12 × 40 = 480 and 10 × 50 = 500, so 980. A stroke along a row groups it.
Phase 2 (figure c): four rows of eight 32s and four rows of four 64s; 32 × 32 = 1024 and 16 × 64 = 1024, two equal halves, so 2048. A second line under the finding says why the halves match.
Phase 3 (figure f): the rings of one number each round 1000: 1000 + 4 × 500 + 8 × 250 + 18 × 125 = 1000 + 2000 + 2000 + 2250 = 7250. The outer ring has 18, which children often miscount.

Phase 4 (dice, figures b then d): each die counts as its dots. Figure b: five blocks of four 5s make 20 × 5 = 100 and the other 44 dice show 1, so 144. Figure d: 17 dice show 3 (both sides and one row near the bottom) and 18 show 4, so 51 + 72 = 123. Each figure has its own hint ladder and its own judged total.

Phase 5 (figure e): every one of the 66 corners holds 15, 25 or 35: each outer hexagon shows one number six times, each blue rhombus one number four times and the middle hexagon each number twice, so each number is written 22 times: 330 + 550 + 770 = 1650 (or 22 × 75).

Phase 6 (create, end Q7): a mirrored board makes any pattern quick to add: each pair counts twice, each middle-line tile once. The target moves in tens from 210 to 390 (all 19 are buildable); any board that makes the target is accepted. A board that misses says what it adds up to.

Free play (reworked 2026-09-30): the sum depends only on how many tiles show each number, never on where they sit. Start it at 12 × 40 + 10 × 50 = 980 (figure a), then press + or − on a row to change how many, −10/−1/+1/+10 to change a number, or new board for a fresh random scenario; the live line, each product and the total follow at once.

Example 2: Figure e: a hexagon made of pieces showing 15, 25 and 35.

3. 15 + 25 + 35 = 75.
4. 22 × 75 = 1650.
Answer: 1650

video_script.anchor: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, ... Why does the rule take every one of them to 1?
video_script.design: One idea: halving undoes doubling, so the rule walks down the list of powers of 2. Assumes: doubling, halving and even numbers. Wrong idea: giving two examples as the reason; broken by the list that never ends. The anchor list stays all video; the block stays from the ground to the idea part; one clear, before the recap.
never_show: 8 and 16 work as a finished reason
every number reaches 1 as a proved fact
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip tries 8 and 16, sees both reach 1, and calls that the reason; the list of powers of 2 runs off the edge of the screen, and the two ticked examples are shown to say nothing about the rest
maths_rules: the powers of 2 from Chapter 1, Table 1: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, ... each double the one before (1 x 2 = 2, 2 x 2 = 4, 4 x 2 = 8, 8 x 2 = 16, 16 x 2 = 32, 32 x 2 = 64)
every power of 2 except 1 is even, because it is 2 times a whole number
half of a power of 2 is the power of 2 before it, because halving undoes the doubling: 64 / 2 = 32, 32 / 2 = 16, 16 / 2 = 8, 8 / 2 = 4, 4 / 2 = 2, 2 / 2 = 1
so the Collatz route from any power of 2 only halves, steps down the list and reaches 1; from 64 it takes 6 halvings
block picture: 64 squares split into two equal halves of 32; one half is kept each time: 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1; every split is into two equal halves with none left over
the check in the recap: 1024 / 2 = 512, 256, 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, which is 10 halvings with no odd number before 1
this proves the rule only for powers of 2; for all whole numbers the conjecture (Collatz, 1937) is still unproved, and the video says so
the book's answer key gives the same reason: dividing 2 x 2 x ... x 2 by 2 removes one 2 each time until 2 / 2 = 1
video_script.payoff_line: No odd number ever comes before one, so every power of two reaches one

final_answer.value: Every power of 2 except 1 is even, and half of a power of 2 is the power of 2 before it (64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1), so no odd number comes before 1 and every power of 2 reaches 1.

media.title: Collatz Path Explorer
media.context: CBSE Class 6, NCERT Ganita Prakash Ch.3 'Number Play', section 3.10 'An Unsolved Mystery: the Collatz Conjecture!' (book pages 68 to 69: sequences a to d, the rule, Collatz's 1937 conjecture, 'Make some more Collatz sequences ... Do you always reach 1? Do you believe the conjecture ...? Why or why not?'), plus the two Collatz questions of the chapter's closing Figure it Out (page 73, Q8 powers of 2 and Q9 start 100) and the Summary line on unsolved problems. Converted from the self-contained HTML build in output/maths/std6/cbse_eng_maths6_ch3_new (tool_collatz_path_explorer, M3.S30.T30.C180.2D1.html); the screen is the same 1600 x 900 stage drawn by the same code, then extended for full NCERT coverage.
media.description: A 1600 x 900 stage with a 'Now' card (the current number and its step count), two big move buttons, ÷ 2 and × 3 + 1, and a bar trail of the path (powers of 2 in their own colour, the peak labelled, an inset of the last 20 steps when a huge peak flattens them). At every step the child chooses the move; a move that does not fit the number's parity is refused with a line saying why (never the answer); a 2nd refusal at the same number shows the answer ('The answer: ÷ 2, because 12 is even'), turns that button green and plays the move. Phase 1: the book's four printed sequences a to d (12, 17, 21, 22) are rebuilt one after another; the book's row stays on screen and each move turns one more of its numbers bold, so the child answers NCERT's 'Do you see how these sequences were formed?' step by step; a side list marks a to d with their step counts (9, 12, 7, 15). Phase 2: the child checks the conjecture for 100 by hand, all 25 steps, the whole path printed. Phase 3: Chapter 1's powers of 2 are recalled on screen; the child halves 64 down to 1 and then chooses why every power of 2 falls straight down (2 × ... × 2, so halving keeps it even until 1); the three reasons are full-width one-line rows; the two tempting ones (they are even, they are big) are answered with 12 and 100, and a 2nd wrong reason shows the right reason green and closes the step. Phase 4: 27 is started with five moves by hand, Auto finishes its 111 steps, and the child slides along the trail and types its peak, 9232, on the keypad (a value on the path, off the path or above the peak each gets its own reason; a 2nd wrong number fills in 9232 in green and moves the slider to step 77). Phase 5: the child predicts which of 12 and 22 takes more steps (a wrong prediction can be tried again; a 2nd wrong one shows 22 in green), then runs both by hand (22: 15, 12: 9). Phase 6: NCERT's 'Do you believe the conjecture of Collatz that all such sequences will eventually reach 1? Why or why not?': the evidence (seven starts and their steps) and Collatz's 1937 guess, still unproved, are on screen, and the child chooses a reason; both reasoned views (every tested start reaches 1 / trying is not proving) are accepted, the reason the child's own paths contradict (every step makes it smaller) is answered with 27, and a 2nd wrong reason shows both accepted reasons green. Finish, the last step's button, opens a celebration (confetti, 'Well done!', the title, the stars with the first-time count, play again); the old finish card and Free play are no longer reachable from the flow (their code is kept). Free play (reworked 2026-09-30) was a live explorer: the child sets a start A (stepper -10 / -1 / +1 / +10, typing on the keypad or keyboard, or New numbers for a fresh random start) and can turn on Compare for a second start B; the whole path, its bar chart (powers of 2 in their own colour, the peak labelled, an inset of the last 20 steps when a huge peak flattens them), the number of steps and the highest number reached update at once on every change, with one live sentence saying what the numbers show ('Make some more Collatz sequences ... favourite whole numbers'). 0 is explained, not run; the limits 1 and 9999 are said on screen. Every step on the step bar (the dots, bottom right) is a button that opens that step.

teaching_notes: Phase 1 (sequences a to d, NCERT p.68): 12, 6, 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 (9 steps); 17 ... 1 (12 steps); 21, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 (7 steps); 22 ... 1 (15 steps). The rule forms every one: even, halve; odd, times 3 plus 1. The book's row stays on screen, so 'Do you see how these sequences were formed?' is answered move by move; a move that does not fit the parity is refused with a question.

Phase 2 (Figure it Out Q9): the conjecture holds for 100: 100, 50, 25, 76, 38, 19, 58, 29, 88, 44, 22, 11, 34, 17, 52, 26, 13, 40, 20, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, 25 steps (the NCERT answer section's sequence).

Phase 3 (Figure it Out Q8): every power of 2 is 2 × 2 × ... × 2, so halving it gives the power of 2 before it and it stays even all the way down to 1: 64 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 falls in 6 halvings, 2^k in k. 'Even' is not enough (12 goes up at 3); 'big' is not it (100 climbs and falls for 25 steps).
Phase 4 (beyond NCERT): 27 takes 111 steps and climbs to 9232 at step 77 before it comes down: a path can climb very high and still reach 1.
Phase 5 (beyond NCERT): 22 takes 15 steps, 12 takes 9; size alone does not decide the length (64 falls in 6, 27 takes 111). A prediction that is not yet right still resolves when the race is run.

Phase 6 (NCERT p.69, 'Do you believe ...? Why or why not?'): an opinion with a reason. Both honest views are accepted: 'every start tested reaches 1' (good evidence, but testing is not proving) and 'a start nobody has tried might never reach 1' (why it is still unsolved). 'Every step makes the number smaller' is not accepted: 27 climbs to 9232. Lothar Collatz guessed it in 1937; nobody has proved it.

Free play (educator feedback 2026-09-30): nothing is judged and there is no Check. Start A and, with Compare on, start B are the only inputs; every output (whole path, chart, steps, highest number, the live sentence) is computed from them on every change, so the child sees cause and effect. Compare starts on the neighbour below A (28 with 27: 18 steps against 111, highest 52 against 9232): starts that sit side by side can take very different paths. Every start tried reaches 1; that is evidence, not proof.

Two tries (2026-10-02): the 1st wrong answer only says why it does not fit; the 2nd shows the answer and closes the question. A move is a question per number (12 is even, so ÷ 2). After a shown answer the child still reaches the next number, step or screen by their own taps.

Example 1: Check the rule on sequence a.

maths_rules: the powers of 2 from Chapter 1, Table 1: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, ... each double the one before (1 x 2 = 2, 2 x 2 = 4, 4 x 2 = 8, 8 x 2 = 16, 16 x 2 = 32, 32 x 2 = 64)
every power of 2 except 1 is even, because it is 2 times a whole number
half of a power of 2 is the power of 2 before it, because halving undoes the doubling: 64 / 2 = 32, 32 / 2 = 16, 16 / 2 = 8, 8 / 2 = 4, 4 / 2 = 2, 2 / 2 = 1
so the Collatz route from any power of 2 only halves, steps down the list and reaches 1; from 64 it takes 6 halvings
block picture: 64 squares split into two equal halves of 32; one half is kept each time: 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1; every split is into two equal halves with none left over
the check in the recap: 1024 / 2 = 512, 256, 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, which is 10 halvings with no odd number before 1
this proves the rule only for powers of 2; for all whole numbers the conjecture (Collatz, 1937) is still unproved, and the video says so
the book's answer key gives the same reason: dividing 2 x 2 x ... x 2 by 2 removes one 2 each time until 2 / 2 = 1

content.text: $1$, $2$, $4$, $8$, $16$, $32$, $64$, ... Why does the rule take every one of them to $1$?
content.question: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, ... Why does the rule take every one of them to 1?
content.question_tex: $1$, $2$, $4$, $8$, $16$, $32$, $64$, ... Why does the rule take every one of them to $1$?
content.publication_text: $1$, $2$, $4$, $8$, $16$, $32$, $64$, ... Why does the rule take every one of them to $1$?

content.text:
$1$. The numbers $1$, $2$, $4$, $8$, $16$, $32$, $64$, ... are the powers of $2$: each is double the one before it.
$2$. Apart from $1$, every one of them is even, so the rule halves it.
$3$. Halving a power of $2$ gives the power of $2$ before it: half of $64$ is $32$, half of $32$ is $16$, and so on.
$4$. So each step moves one place back along the list: $64$, $32$, $16$, $8$, $4$, $2$, $1$.
$5$. No odd number appears before $1$, so the rule never has to multiply by $3$ and add $1$.
$6$. So the sequence keeps moving back along the list until it reaches $1$; for example $64$ takes $6$ steps.
Answer: Every power of $2$ except $1$ is even, so the rule halves it and moves one place back along the list. No odd number appears on the way, so it always reaches $1$.

media.title: Estimate Builder
media.context: CBSE Class 6, NCERT Ganita Prakash Ch.3 'Number Play', section 3.11 'Simple Estimation' (book pages 69 to 71: the worked example, Figure it Out Q1 to Q3, Estimate the answer Q1 to Q7), plus the two estimation questions of the chapter-end Figure it Out on page 72 (Q4 holidays in a year, Q5 litres in a mug, a bucket and an overhead tank). Converted from the self-contained HTML build in output/maths/std6/cbse_eng_maths6_ch3_new (tool_estimate_builder, M4.S32.T32.C187.2D1.html), whose four claims are kept as parts, then extended to every estimation question of the section; the screen is the same 1600 x 900 stage drawn by the same code.
media.description: An estimate is built from parts the child knows. Each part of the tool shows NCERT's question, a number line, a chain of up to three rows and a palette of blocks. The child taps blocks into the chain; each block is a unit fraction (students per section, km in an hour) and the chain's units are worked out live: unit words that cancel are struck through and what is left must read the question's units, or the chain shows 'units clash' with the clashing words in coral. Rough blocks carry a slider for the child's own value (the students in their section, their breaths in a minute, the metres to their door); exact blocks (60 minutes in an hour, 1000 m in a km) do not. Chains multiply, add (costs, holidays) or divide (walking time = distance ÷ km in an hour ÷ hours walked a day; a divisor's unit words turn over). Once the units match, the estimate appears on the number line and the child answers: judges a claim Too high / About right / Too low (Paromita's 500 students, Sheetal's 13,000 hours, a friend's 2000 breaths a day, Roshan's ₹100 custard), picks more or less than a number (bus riders and 200, textbook words and 5000, each with a quick guess first), the nearest of NCERT's 150, 400 or a thousand, a few thousand or over 10,000 (grains of rice on a plate, in a 1 kg bag), or presses Check my estimate. The sensible range then appears as a green band with a line saying how it was built. An answer about the child's own world (their school, their bus riders, Roshan's shopping) is checked against the child's OWN chain, so every sensible value is accepted. Six phases, 23 parts, in NCERT's order: at school (4), steps to walk a to d (4), breaths in a minute, an hour and a day (3), a few thousand or more (3), near and far: Gandhinagar to Kohima on a map line with 250 km gaps, then walking times to a place nearby, a neighbouring state's capital and the length of India (4), and at home: Roshan's custard, holidays in a year then the exact number from the school calendar on a keypad, and the litres in a mug, a bucket and an overhead tank, each built from the one before (5). Two tries, then the answer: a wrong answer says why it does not fit and nothing more (the sensible range stays hidden, the verdict is not in getState, and that button greys out until the chain or a value changes); the second wrong answer on the same part shows the answer, in the caption ('The answer: ...') and in the green card with the range on the line, and closes the part, counted as not first time; on a part where the child sets a value (the gaps on the map) the second miss instead shows one worked example small at the right end of the task card ('9 gaps = 2250 km'), leaves the child's slider where it is, and the part finishes when the child sets it. A finished part shows 'next part'. Finish on the last step opens a celebration card (confetti, 'Well done!', stars from the parts answered right first time, play again). Free play (eight block sets with multiply, add or divide, nothing judged) is still in the code, but no screen opens it any more.

tool_config.screen: A claim card at the top with a marker on a number line, a chain of factor blocks with rough sliders, and the estimate shown as a shaded band on the same line.
feedback: The tool shows the band of reasonable estimates and whether the claim sits inside it.
A block that does not belong (for example minutes for a daily count) makes the units label clash.
tool_config.one_idea: An estimate is built from known parts multiplied together, and it gives a sensible range, not one number.
tool_config.done_when: Four claims are judged with a reasoned chain of blocks.

Set each slider to a sensible rough value.
Compare the estimate band with the claim marker.
Press Too high, About right or Too low.

teaching_notes: Phase 1, at school: Paromita's sections have 32, 29 and 35 children (about 100 a class) and Classes 6 to 10 have 3 sections each, so about 33 × 3 × 5 ≈ 500: About right. Then the child's own school (students per section × sections per class × classes, nearest of 150, 400, 1000), bus riders (buses × children per bus, more or less than 200, guess first), and Sheetal: 6 h × 200 days = 1200 h a year; 13,000 ÷ 1200 ≈ 11 years but she has had about 8 (nursery, KG, 1 to 6): Too high.

Phase 2, steps (Figure it Out Q1 a to d): steps = metres × steps in a metre (a child's step is about half a metre, so about 2 a metre); for school to home the km first become metres (× 1000). Every sensible value is accepted; the band says how the range was built.

Phase 3, breaths (Figure it Out Q2 a to c): count breaths for a minute (12 to 20 at rest), × 60 for an hour (720 to 1200), × 24 for a day (about 17,000 to 29,000; 15 × 60 × 24 = 21,600), so a friend's 2000 a day is Too low. The chain keeps its blocks from part to part.

Phase 4, a few thousand or more (Figure it Out Q3, Estimate the answer Q1): a plate needs 50 to 100 g of rice at 40 to 60 grains a gram: 2000 to 6000 grains, a few thousand; a 1 kg bag is 1000 g: 40,000 to 60,000, over 10,000. Words in the textbook: 8 to 12 a line × 20 to 35 lines × 150 to 300 pages is at least 24,000, far more than 5000 (guess within 30 seconds, then check).

Phase 5, near and far (Estimate the answer Q4, Q6): Gandhinagar to Kohima is about 2200 km in a straight line (almost 9 gaps of 250 km on the map line) and about 3000 km by road; 2000 to 3000 km is accepted, NCERT says about 2500 km. Walking time divides: metres ÷ metres a minute = minutes; km ÷ km an hour ÷ hours walked a day = days (India, about 3200 km south to north, at 40 km a day is 80 days).

Phase 6, at home (Estimate the answer Q3, chapter-end Q4, Q5): Roshan's milk (₹40 to ₹70) + three fruits (₹45 to ₹150) is ₹85 to ₹220, so ₹100 is About right only with small servings and cheap fruit (judged against the child's own chain, as NCERT's answer allows both). Holidays: 52 Sundays + festivals + vacation, a little over 110, then the exact number from the calendar and how close it was. Litres: a mug about 1, a bucket 10 to 40 (mugs × litres a mug), a tank 500 to 2000 (buckets × litres a bucket).

topics.summary: When an exact count is not needed, a good estimate is. We build estimates from parts we know, judge whether a claim is reasonable and compare estimates with exact counts.

video_script.anchor: About how many holidays in a year?
video_script.design: One idea: an estimate is built from parts you can count roughly. Assumes: weeks in a year and adding. Wrong idea: counting only festivals. The year strip stays on the stage from the ground to the idea part; one clear, before the recap.
never_show: one exact count presented as the answer for every school
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip counts only the festival days. On the year strip, all the Sundays and the long vacation blocks light up, far more than fifteen, so the count is struck through.
maths_rules: a year has 365 days, which is 52 weeks and 1 day (52 x 7 = 364), so a year has 52 or 53 Sundays: about 52
festival and national holidays: about 15; the number differs from school to school and state to state
vacations: a summer vacation of about 6 weeks (42 days) plus a few shorter breaks: about 50 days
52 + 15 + 50 = 117, a little over 110; easier rounding: 50 + 15 + 50 = 115

a Sunday that falls inside a vacation is one holiday, not two: about 7 Sundays sit inside a 50-day vacation (50 / 7 is about 7), so the true total is a little lower, about 117 - 7 = 110; the estimate is a range, about 110 to 120
if the school also closes on Saturdays, add about 52 more: 117 + 52 = 169, about 170
The slip's about 15 counts only the festival days and misses the 52 Sundays and the 50 vacation days
the exact count comes from each child's own school calendar; the video gives no single exact number
video_script.payoff_line: About one hundred and ten to one hundred and twenty holidays is a good estimate

final_answer.value: about 110 to 120 holidays, then checked against the school calendar
final_answer.spoken: about one hundred and ten to one hundred and twenty holidays

video_script.substitution: Split the holidays into Sundays, festival days and vacations, round each part and add.
video_script.wrong_answer: Holidays are festival days, so about fifteen

video_script.design: One idea: build from a known litre to bigger containers by counting how many fit. Assumes: a litre bottle and multiplying by 20. Wrong idea: judging the tank by its look. The three containers stay in a row on the stage all video; one clear, before the recap.
never_show: 50 litres marked as the tank's size
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip guesses the tank holds about 50 litres because it looks only a bit bigger than a bucket. 50 litres is only two and a half buckets, drawn next to the tank, far fewer than a tank holds, so the guess is struck through.
maths_rules: a big water bottle holds 1 litre; the bathing mug holds about as much, about 1 litre (a small cup is much less; this is a big mug)
a bucket fills with about 15 to 20 mugs, so a bucket holds about 15 to 20 litres, about 20 litres
an overhead tank fills with about 25 to 50 buckets of 20 litres: 25 x 20 = 500 and 50 x 20 = 1000, so about 500 to 1000 litres
many plastic roof tanks have their size in litres printed on the side, often 500 or 1000
The slip's 50 litres is 50 / 20 = 2 and a half buckets, far fewer buckets than a tank holds

every drawing keeps the order: mug about the size of the 1 litre bottle, bucket bigger than the mug, tank much bigger than the bucket; sizes are shown by counting containers, never by a drawn height alone
video_script.payoff_line: About one litre, about twenty litres, and about five hundred to one thousand litres

final_answer.value: mug about 1 litre, bucket about 20 litres, tank about 500 to 1000 litres
final_answer.spoken: about one litre, about twenty litres, and about five hundred to one thousand litres

video_script.substitution: Start from a one litre bottle, then count how many of each smaller container fill the next bigger one.

content.question: Paromita estimates the number of students in her school.
content.question_tex: Paromita estimates the number of students in her school.
content.publication_text: Paromita estimates the number of students in her school.

content.text:
$1$. Her section has $32$ children and the other two have $29$ and $35$.
$2$. $32 + 29 + 35$ is about $100$, so her class has about $100$ children.
$3$. The school has Classes $6$ to $10$, which is $5$ classes, each with $3$ sections.
$4$. Assuming about $100$ in each class: $5 \times 100 = 500$.
Answer: About $500$ students.

Assuming about 100 in each class: 5 × 100 = 500.

content.text: Estimate the number of holidays in a year, then count exactly.
content.question: Estimate the number of holidays in a year, then count exactly.
content.question_tex: Estimate the number of holidays in a year, then count exactly.
content.publication_text: Estimate the number of holidays in a year, then count exactly.

content.text:
$1$. Sundays: about $52$.
$2$. Festival and national holidays: about $15$.
$3$. Vacations: about $50$ days.
$4$. Estimate: about $52 + 15 + 50$, a little over $110$.
$5$. Then count exactly from your school calendar and compare.
Answer: An estimate of about $110$ to $120$, checked against the calendar.

Festival and national holidays: about 15.
Vacations: about 50 days.

content.text: Estimate how many litres a mug, a bucket and an overhead tank hold.
content.question: Estimate how many litres a mug, a bucket and an overhead tank hold.
content.question_tex: Estimate how many litres a mug, a bucket and an overhead tank hold.
content.publication_text: Estimate how many litres a mug, a bucket and an overhead tank hold.

content.text:
$1$. A mug holds about as much as a big water bottle: about $1$ litre.
$2$. A bucket fills about $15$ to $20$ mugs: about $15$ to $20$ litres.
$3$. An overhead tank fills many buckets: often $500$ to $1000$ litres.
Answer: About $1$ litre, about $20$ litres and about $500$ to $1000$ litres.

A bucket fills about 15 to 20 mugs: about 15 to 20 litres.
An overhead tank fills many buckets: often 500 to 1000 litres.

video_script.anchor: Gandhinagar to Kohima: about how many kilometres?
video_script.design: One idea: a map's scale bar turns a map line into kilometres. Assumes: reading a map and multiplying by 500. Wrong idea: guessing small because both cities are in India. The map stays on the stage from the ground to the idea part; one clear, before the recap.
never_show: 200 km marked as a sensible answer
an exact road distance presented as the answer
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip guesses 200 km because both cities are in India. A 200 km piece is laid on the line between the cities and covers less than half of one 500 km scale bar, a tiny part of the whole line, so the guess is struck through.
maths_rules: the map of India is a plain outline drawn to one true scale; both cities sit at their true positions: Gandhinagar about 23.2 N, 72.6 E; Kohima about 25.7 N, 94.1 E
the scale bar stands for 500 km at the scale of the map
the straight line from Gandhinagar to Kohima is about 2190 km (great-circle distance with Earth radius 6371 km gives 2188 km)
2188 / 500 = 4.38, so the bar fits 4 times with a little left over; 4 x 500 = 2000; the straight line is a little over 2000 km
roads bend, so the real trip is longer than the straight line; a sensible estimate is anything from 2000 to 3000 km; the book's answer is about 2500 km
The slip's 200 km is 200 / 500 = 2/5 of one bar, less than half a bar; 200 / 2188 is less than 1/10 of the line
check: India is about 3000 km wide from west to east (about 2933 km); the two cities sit a little in from the west and east edges, so the straight line is big but less than the whole width
no exact road distance is claimed or shown
video_script.payoff_line: About two thousand five hundred kilometres is a good estimate

final_answer.value: about 2500 km (anything from 2000 to 3000 km is sensible)
final_answer.spoken: about two thousand five hundred kilometres

video_script.design: One idea: build the estimate from parts, then compare it with the claim. Assumes: multiplying by 6, by 200 and by 8. Wrong idea: counting every day of the year as a school day. maths_rules: the claim: about 13,000 hours in school till date, for a child in Grade 6 (called Class 6 in the video)
a school day is about 6 hours; a year has about 200 school days (the book's answer key uses the same two numbers)
6 x 200 = 1200 hours in a school year
Class 1 to Class 6 is 6 years: 1200 x 6 = 7200 hours
with 2 more years of nursery and kindergarten, 8 years: 1200 x 8 = 9600 hours
so a good estimate is about 7000 to 10,000 hours; 13,000 is more than this, so it is too many
The slip: 6 hours on all 365 days for 6 years: 6 x 365 = 2190; 2190 x 6 = 13,140, a little over 13,000
backwards check: 13,000 / 1200 is about 10.8, so about 11 years of school, far more than a Class 6 child has had (the book's answer key gives 10.8 years)
item 7 (make your own estimation questions) is covered in the recap as the child's own task; no numbers are given for it

final_answer.value: No: about 7000 to 10,000 hours, so 13,000 is too many.
final_answer.spoken: no, thirteen thousand hours is too many

media.teaching_notes: The one idea: build a quick estimate from parts you know and see whether the claim fits. Watch for the slip of counting all 365 days of the year as school days, which gives about 13,140 hours and makes the claim look right.

media.description: The book asks how long it would take to walk to a favourite place nearby, to a neighbouring state's capital, and from the southernmost point of India to the northernmost. At about 5 km in each hour, 1 km takes about 12 minutes; a place 2 km away takes about half an hour, a capital about 300 km away takes about 60 hours, and the over 3000 km across India takes over 600 hours.

video_script.anchor: Walking at about 5 km an hour: how long to each place?
video_script.design: One idea: time for a walk is how many fives fit into the distance, in hours. Assumes: sharing into fives. Wrong idea: thinking a long walk fits in a day. The walking-speed card stays in the anchor all video; the road picture is cleared once, before the recap.
never_show: 300 km walked in one day, marked as possible
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip says the 300 km to a neighbouring capital can be walked in one day. A day's walk of 10 hours covers 10 x 5 = 50 km, drawn as a short piece at the start of the 300 km road, one sixth of it, so the claim is struck through.
maths_rules: walking pace: about 5 km in one hour (a normal pace); 60 minutes / 5 = 12 minutes for each km
a. a favourite place nearby is taken as 2 km away: 2 x 12 = 24 minutes, about half an hour; this distance is chosen for the video, each child uses their own place
b. a neighbouring state's capital is taken as about 300 km away, a round number for the video: 300 / 5 = 60 hours; walking 8 hours a day, 60 / 8 = 7.5 days, about a week

c. from the southernmost point of India to the northernmost point is over 3000 km (India's north to south extent is usually given as 3214 km); 3000 / 5 = 600 hours, so over 600 hours; walking 8 hours a day, 600 / 8 = 75 days, well over two months
The slip's day: even 10 hours of walking is 10 x 5 = 50 km, one sixth of 300 km
check by multiplying back: 60 hours x 5 km = 300 km; 600 hours x 5 km = 3000 km
every road length drawn is to one scale: 50 km is one sixth of the 300 km road
video_script.payoff_line: About half an hour, about sixty hours, and over six hundred hours

final_answer.value: a. about 24 minutes for a place 2 km away; b. about 60 hours for a capital about 300 km away; c. over 600 hours for over 3000 km
final_answer.spoken: about half an hour, about sixty hours, and over six hundred hours

content.question: Words in your maths book: more than 5000, or less than 5000?
content.question_tex: Words in your maths book: more than $5000$, or less than $5000$?
content.publication_text: Words in your maths book: more than $5000$, or less than $5000$?

content.text:
$1$. Sample answer: an estimate built from parts; your numbers may differ.
$2$. A full page has a few hundred words, but pictures and blank space take room, so take a low guess of $100$ words on a page.
$3$. The book has well over $100$ pages, so take $100$ pages.
$4$. $100 \times 100 = 10,000$ words.
$5$. Even this low guess is more than $5000$.
Answer: More than $5000$: a low estimate gives about $10,000$ words.

content.text: Students who come to school by bus: more than $200$, or less than $200$?
content.question: Students who come to school by bus: more than 200, or less than 200?
content.question_tex: Students who come to school by bus: more than $200$, or less than $200$?
content.publication_text: Students who come to school by bus: more than $200$, or less than $200$?

content.text:
$1$. Sample answer: this depends on your school, so here is one way to estimate.
$2$. One school bus carries about $40$ students.
$3$. Count the buses that come to the school; suppose there are $6$.
$4$. $6 \times 40 = 240$ students.
$5$. $240$ is more than $200$, so for $6$ buses the answer is more than $200$.
$6$. With only $4$ buses it would be $4 \times 40 = 160$, which is less than $200$, so the answer changes with the number of buses.
Answer: Sample answer: for $6$ buses about $240$ students, which is more than $200$; it depends on how many buses your school has.

content.text: Gandhinagar to Kohima: about how many kilometres?
content.question: Gandhinagar to Kohima: about how many kilometres?
content.question_tex: Gandhinagar to Kohima: about how many kilometres?
content.publication_text: Gandhinagar to Kohima: about how many kilometres?

content.text:
$1$. Sample answer: estimate from the map of India, because the two towns are nearly at opposite ends.
$2$. India is about $3000\text{ km}$ wide from west to east.
$3$. Gandhinagar is a little in from the western edge and Kohima a little in from the eastern edge.
$4$. Take off about $250\text{ km}$ at each end: $3000 - 250 - 250 = 2500\text{ km}$.
$5$. Taking off $400\text{ km}$ at each end gives $3000 - 400 - 400 = 2200\text{ km}$, so the estimate lies between about $2200$ and $2500\text{ km}$.
$6$. A road journey winds about, so by road it is longer than the straight line on the map.
Answer: Sample answer: about $2500\text{ km}$ in a straight line on the map (anything near $2200$ to $2500\text{ km}$ is a good estimate).

content.text: Sheetal is in Grade $6$ and says she has spent about $13,000$ hours in school. Do you agree?

content.text:
$1$. School is about $6$ hours a day.
$2$. There are about $200$ school days a year: $6 \times 200 = 1200$ hours a year.
$3$. Grades $1$ to $6$ is $6$ years: $1200 \times 6 = 7200$ hours.
$4$. Even adding $2$ years of pre-school, $1200 \times 8 = 9600$ hours.
Answer: No: about $7000$ to $10,000$ hours, so $13,000$ is too many.

content.text: How long would it take you to walk across India?
content.question: How long would it take you to walk across India?
content.question_tex: How long would it take you to walk across India?
content.publication_text: How long would it take you to walk across India?

content.text:
$1$. Sample answer: your walking speed and daily walking time may differ.
$2$. Across India, for example from south to north, is over $3000\text{ km}$; use $3000\text{ km}$.
$3$. A walking speed is about $5\text{ km}$ each hour.
$4$. Hours of walking: $3000 \div 5 = 600$ hours.
$5$. Walking about $8$ hours a day: $600 \div 8 = 75$ days.
$6$. $75$ days is about two and a half months; allowing for winding roads and rest days, it is nearer $3$ months.
Answer: Sample answer: about $600$ hours of walking, which is about $75$ days at $8$ hours a day, so around $3$ months with rest days.

media.title: Race-to-N Arena
media.context: CBSE Class 6, NCERT Ganita Prakash Ch.3 'Number Play', section 3.12 'Games and Winning Strategies' (book pages 71 to 72: Game #1, the game of 21; Game #2, the race to 99; making your own variations) and the end-of-chapter Figure it Out Q10 (page 73: the race to 22 from 0). The other end-of-chapter questions (Q1 to Q9) are on the chapter's other topics and belong to the sibling tools listed in ncertCoverage. Converted from the self-contained HTML build in output/maths/std6/cbse_eng_maths6_ch3_new (tool_race_to_n_arena, M4.S35.T35.C208.2D1.html); the screen is the same 1600 x 900 stage drawn by the same code, then extended for NCERT coverage (2026-09-29).
media.description: A board of numbered squares from 0 to the target, laid out as a snake so every square stays big enough to tap, fills the left of the stage; the right column shows the number said, the target, the move buttons (add 1 up to the largest move), a Mark safe pencil, new game, and the numbers each player has said. Phase 1 (NCERT Game #1, the game of 21, adding 1, 2 or 3): the child goes first against a computer that plays at random until the child has lost twice, then perfectly; a win counts only if the child took a safe number whenever one was in reach (1, then 5, 9, 13, 17, 21), and a loss or an unsafe win says why and asks for another game (the green rings are the answer, so they are not shown after a miss). After the winning game the child answers NCERT's two questions: which player can always win if they play correctly (the first player), then the pattern of numbers the winner should say, marked square by square with the pencil and checked (1, 5, 9, 13, 17, with 21 optional); the green rings appear only once the pattern is right. Phase 2 (NCERT Game #2, the race to 99 adding 1 to 10): the computer is perfect from the start, so the child, going first, loses; then the child answers that the second player can always win and marks the pattern 11, 22, 33, ..., 88 (99 optional). Phase 3 (end-of-chapter Figure it Out Q10, the race to 22 from 0 adding 1 to 3): win going first by adding 2, then the same two questions (the first player; 2, 6, 10, 14, 18). Phase 4 (make your own variation): set the target (10 to 100) and the largest move (2 to 10), predict whether the first or the second player can always win, then play it with either player first against the perfect computer; the green rings show the safe numbers. Two tries, then the answer: a first wrong answer says only why (an extra mark is named, a missing one is counted); a second wrong answer on the same question shows the answer, in the pill and on the board (a choice: the right one turns green and the next item opens; a pattern or a game: one working example appears small at the right end of the task card and the child makes it themselves, nothing of theirs moves). The finish is a celebration card (confetti, 'Well done!', the stars, play again); the old findings list and free play (reworked 2026-09-30) are no longer reachable from it, their code stays. One idea throughout: working backwards from the target, the safe numbers are spaced by the largest move plus one, and whoever can say them wins.

teaching_notes: Phase 1 (game of 21, add 1 to 3): working back from 21 in steps of 4 gives the safe numbers 17, 13, 9, 5, 1. Whoever says one of them can always reach the next, because whatever the other player adds (1, 2 or 3), you add what makes 4. The first player can always win by saying 1. The computer plays at random until the child has lost twice, then perfectly; a win without keeping to the safe numbers is not accepted ('a better player would have beaten you'). Then: who can always win (the first player) and the pattern (1, 5, 9, 13, 17, 21), marked on the board.

Phase 2 (race to 99, add 1 to 10): the safe numbers are 11 apart: 11, 22, 33, ..., 88, 99. 99 is a multiple of 11, so the count back ends exactly at 0: the first player can never say a safe number first, and the second player, answering each move to make 11, always wins. The perfect computer shows it; the child names the second player and marks 11, 22, ..., 88.

Phase 3 (race to 22 from 0, add 1 to 3; end-of-chapter Q10): 22 counted back in fours gives 18, 14, 10, 6, 2. 22 is not a multiple of 4, so the first player wins by adding 2 first, then landing on 6, 10, 14, 18 and 22. NCERT's answer: 'Winning strategy is to be the first player.'

Phase 4 (your own variation): safe numbers are spaced by the largest move plus one. If the target is a multiple of (largest move + 1), the count back ends at 0 and the second player can always win; otherwise the first player can, starting with the remainder. The default 30 with largest move 4 is a second-player game (30 = 6 x 5). The prediction is judged for whatever target and move the child sets.

$1$. $21$ wins.
$2$. $17$: the opponent reaches $18$ to $20$, and you reach $21$.

the track shows 0 to 22 as 23 equal squares in a row
from 18 the other player reaches 19, 20 or 21, and you add 3, 2 or 1 to reach 22; so 18 is safe
whatever the other player adds (1, 2 or 3), you add the rest of 4 (3, 2 or 1); so safe numbers are 4 apart
0 + 2 = 2, so the first player can reach the first safe number on the first move, and wins

check: each safe number is 4 more than the one before: 2 + 4 = 6, 6 + 4 = 10, 10 + 4 = 14, 14 + 4 = 18, 18 + 4 = 22

topics.summary: Numbers convey information, make patterns, estimate sizes, pose puzzles and win games. Set procedures for using numbers are computational thinking, and some easy-to-pose problems are still unsolved.

content.text: Numbers can be used for many different purposes: to convey information (taller neighbours, supercells), to make and discover patterns (digit sums, palindromes, number lines), to estimate magnitudes, to pose and solve puzzles, and to play and win games.
content.publication_text: Numbers can be used for many different purposes: to convey information (taller neighbours, supercells), to make and discover patterns (digit sums, palindromes, number lines), to estimate magnitudes, to pose and solve puzzles, and to play and win games.

content.text: Thinking about and formulating set procedures to use numbers for these purposes is a useful skill called computational thinking: Kaprekar's routine, reverse-and-add, the Collatz rule and the backwards search for safe numbers are all set procedures.
content.publication_text: Thinking about and formulating set procedures to use numbers for these purposes is a useful skill called computational thinking: Kaprekar's routine, reverse-and-add, the Collatz rule and the backwards search for safe numbers are all set procedures.

content.text: Many problems about numbers are very easy to pose but very difficult to solve; some, such as the Collatz conjecture and whether 196 ever becomes a palindrome, are still unsolved.
