objectives.objective_text: Students read the taller-neighbour rule from two line-ups and use it to find the number each child says, including why an end child says only 0 or 1.
Students decide whether a sequence of numbers is possible for a line of children, justifying each answer with the tallest child, who always says 0, and the end children, who never say 2.
Students recall the three facts of the rule and arrange children of different heights to make target sequences, naming the reason when a sequence is impossible.
Students find the rule behind the coloured cells and mark every supercell in a row by comparing each number with its neighbours, remembering an end cell has only one.
Students fill rows so chosen cells become supercells, reach the most supercells possible (half the cells, rounded up), and explain why the largest number is always a supercell and the smallest never.
Students find supercells in a grid using left, right, top and bottom neighbours, and complete a grid with 5-digit numbers made from given digits, written with commas.
Students solve a grid puzzle by swapping two digits to make four supercells, and design rows and grids whose supercells fall exactly on marked cells.
Students place 4-digit numbers on a line marked in thousands by finding the two marks they lie between and which one they are nearer to.
Students work out the step of a number line from two labelled ticks, label every tick, and mark the smallest and largest numbers as the leftmost and rightmost.
Students use order and distance on the line to find the largest, smallest and closest-to-50,000 odd-digit numbers, and set line steps and place numbers accurately.
Students count the numbers with 1 to 5 digits as 9, 90, 900, 9000 and 90,000, using 9 choices for the first digit and 10 for every other place.
Students count how often the digit 7 is written from 1 to 100 and from 1 to 1000 by counting each place separately, so that 77 counts twice.
Students apply place-by-place counting to find every 7 in a hundred grid, sorting each by its place, and extend the count to 1 to 1000.
Students find digit sums, build the smallest number (59) and largest 5-digit number (95,000) with digit sum 14, and explain why no largest number with that digit sum exists.
Students explain why digit sums rise by 1 and drop by 8 at each new ten, and why numbers with consecutive digits have a digit sum three times the middle digit.
Students set digits to reach a target digit sum and to make the smallest and largest numbers with it, checking each attempt against the true extreme.
Students define a palindrome, test numbers by checking that their digits mirror about the middle, and list all nine 3-digit palindromes made from 1, 2 and 3.
Students carry out reverse-and-add until a palindrome appears, count the rounds, and state that 2-digit starts always succeed while 196 is still unsettled.
Students use the mirror structure to solve the 12421 puzzle and to find the sum and difference of the smallest and largest 5-digit palindromes, then run reverse-and-add on new starts.
Students find all times of three patterns on a 12-hour clock, including the 57 palindromic times, and count the minutes between them, such as 70 minutes from 10:01 to 11:11.
Students build dates with repeating or palindromic digits, check them by reversing all eight digits, and use weekday shifts after ordinary and leap years to find when a calendar is reused.
Students apply the time, date and weekday-shift rules to new cases, marking every palindromic time on a moving clock and stating the minutes between them.
Students describe D. R. Kaprekar's discovery, form the largest and smallest numbers from four digits to compare their sums and differences, and carry out his routine from 6382 to 6174.
Students keep four digits at every step, including leading zeros, count the rounds for numbers such as 5683 and their birth year, and find that 3-digit numbers settle at 495.
Students state the steps and rules of Kaprekar's routine and run it round by round on new starts, arranging the digits correctly each round until 6174 or 495 appears.
Students make targets from given numbers by adding and repeating them, and explain why 1000 cannot be made while 14,000, 15,000, 16,000 and every other thousand can.
Students make targets such as 39,800, 45,000 and 21,400 by both adding and subtracting given numbers.
Students match the big part first, then reuse or subtract smaller numbers, to build new targets and to declare impossible ones with a reason.
Students use the smallest and largest numbers of each length to decide whether each requested sum or difference is possible, giving an example or a reason.
Students classify digit-count statements as always, sometimes or never true, backing sometimes with examples and never with an extreme case.
Students build numbers to a set total, such as one 5-digit and two 3-digit numbers adding to 18,670, and test new digit-count claims at their extremes.
Students count how many times each number appears in a pattern and multiply instead of adding one by one, finding totals such as 980, 144 and 2048.
Students total patterns built from rings and symmetric parts by adding one part and repeating it, and compare classmates' methods to judge which is quickest.
Students create a pattern whose numbers add up to a chosen total between 210 and 390, and total new patterns by grouping equal numbers.
Students find the rule behind four sequences, state it (halve if even, 3n + 1 if odd), and write sequences for their own starts, confirming that 100 reaches 1 in 25 steps.
Students explain why every power of 2 falls straight to 1, and why many starts reaching 1 still do not prove Collatz's 1937 conjecture, which remains unsolved.
Students apply the rule step by step to new starts, choosing the correct move each time, and compare the length and peak of different paths.
Students tell when an estimate is enough and estimate quantities such as a school's size, steps, blinks and breaths by rounding parts and scaling up.
Students judge whether claims such as 13,000 school hours or a ₹100 custard are reasonable, backing each judgement with a quick estimate.
Students estimate the holidays in a year and the capacity of a mug, a bucket and a tank, and compare an estimate's range with a claim or an exact count.
Students play the game of 21, work backwards from 21 to the safe numbers 17, 13, 9, 5 and 1, and explain why the first player can always win.
Students find the safe numbers for the race to 99 and for new variations such as reaching 22, and decide which player can always win each game.
Students apply working backwards to name the winner of any race-to-a-number game and play to win from the seat the strategy predicts.
Students recall how numbers were used in this chapter to convey information, find patterns, estimate, solve puzzles and win games, and name problems that remain unsolved.

how_to_use.intro: Number Play is computational thinking with whole numbers. Each section is a small world with a rule in it. The child discovers the rule, runs it by hand, notices a pattern and then reasons about what is always, sometimes or never true. Every topic follows the same arc: play first, notice, name, reason about extremes, apply.
